document.content:
{
  "thread_id": "kp-20270322-upgrade-001",
  "mailbox_owner": "kimberly_park",
  "subject": "Private deployment: upgrade comms, phased rollout & rollback matrix",
  "participants_internal": [
    "kimberly_park",
    "mateo_alvarez",
    "karthik_iyer",
    "neha_kapoor",
    "dylan_brooks"
  ],
  "participants_external": [
    "Cameron Blake <cameron@acmecloud.com>",
    "BigBank SecOps <audits@bigbank.com>"
  ],
  "message_count": "5",
  "first_email_at": "2027-03-22T09:14:00-07:00",
  "last_email_at": "2027-03-23T11:05:00-07:00",
  "thread_type": "security_compliance",
  "related_account": "BigBank Corp",
  "region": "us",
  "has_attachments": "true",
  "attachments": [
    "upgrade_matrix_v2.xlsx",
    "comm_plan_draft.md",
    "acme_vpc_routes.png"
  ],
  "related_links": [
    "https://calendar.redwood.com/event/3b9f-upgrade-window",
    "https://docs.redwood.com/private/upgrade-runbook-v2"
  ],
  "messages": [
    "From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>\\nTo: Mateo Alvarez <mateo_alvarez@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>, Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.ai>, Dylan Brooks <dylan_brooks@redwood.ai>\\nCc: Cameron Blake <cameron@acmecloud.com>\\nDate: 2027-03-22T09:14:00-07:00\\nSubject: Private deployment: upgrade comms, phased rollout & rollback matrix\\n\\nTeam \u2014\\n\\nPer BigBank's request we need to schedule the next Private runtime patch (v3.2.1 -> v3.3.0) for their on-prem/VPC deployment and lock down a clear communications and rollback plan. Draft attached: \\\"upgrade_matrix_v2.xlsx\\\" + a short comms draft in \\\"comm_plan_draft.md\\\". High-level asks below so we can finalize before Friday: \\n\\n- Proposed maintenance window: Sat Mar 27 01:00\u201305:00 PT (4h) with a 1h canary phase followed by bulk cutover.\\n- Version pinning: customer currently pinned to 3.2.1; we will propose a soft pin to 3.3.0 for 30 days post-upgrade, with automatic fallback to 3.2.1 if health signals fail.\\n- Rollback criteria (initial): CPU/GPU mem > 85% sustained for 10m, p99 latency degradation > 40%, error rate increase > 3x baseline, or failed KV cache warmup after canary.\\n- Network changes: small route table change to support new sidecar metrics; CAM needs to confirm no IP conflicts.\\n- Audit/compliance: ensure audit logs for config changes and a KMS key rotation window is scheduled with Neha.\\n\\nPlease review the matrix and suggest edits inline. Specific asks: \\n  * Mateo \u2014 confirm canary cluster size and gate thresholds.\\n  * Karthik \u2014 ops orchestration steps and any preflight health checks we should add.\\n  * Neha \u2014 compliance gating and evidence we must provide to BigBank.\\n  * Dylan \u2014 runbook owner for rollback; include checklist for snapshot/restore.\\n\\nIf we agree on Sat 27, I'll send the official notice to BigBank and schedule the 01:00 calendar invite.\\n\\nThanks,\\nKimberly\\n\\n--\\nKimberly Park\\nSenior Program Manager, Private Deployments\\nRedwood Inference\\n",
    "From: Mateo Alvarez <mateo_alvarez@redwood.ai>\\nTo: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>, Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.ai>, Dylan Brooks <dylan_brooks@redwood.ai>\\nCc: Cameron Blake <cameron@acmecloud.com>\\nDate: 2027-03-22T10:03:00-07:00\\nSubject: Re: Private deployment: upgrade comms, phased rollout & rollback matrix\\n\\nKimberly \u2014 quick read through the matrix. A few notes: \\n\\n1) Canary sizing: recommend 10% of production capacity or a minimum of 2 GPU nodes (whichever is higher) for 60m. That gives us prefix/KV cache warmup observation without fully exposing all traffic.\\n2) Gate thresholds: add a third gate for model-level token divergence (automated prompt smoke tests) \u2014 if generation quality drops by > 8% on our golden prompts, fail canary.\\n3) Snapshot cadence: ensure we take both L0 (VM) and model checkpoint snapshots pre-cutover. If snapshot+restore time > 45m for BigBank infra, schedule extra buffer.\\n\\nAlso suggest adding a nightly preflight run for three nights prior to the window to validate images and sidecar versions on a staging clone. I'll update the workbook with canary numbers.\\n\\nOn the rollback approach: prefer a staged rollback (canary -> region -> full) rather than full immediate revert unless critical. Dylan, can you confirm the rollback playbook includes automatic drain and token blackhole steps?\\n\\nMateo\\nPrincipal Site Reliability Engineer\\n",
    "From: Cameron Blake <cameron@acmecloud.com>\\nTo: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>, Mateo Alvarez <mateo_alvarez@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>\\nDate: 2027-03-22T13:21:00-07:00\\nSubject: Re: Private deployment: upgrade comms, phased rollout & rollback matrix\\n\\nThanks for the heads up, Kimberly. A couple of constraints from our side (BigBank's VPC team):\\n\\n- Blackout windows: BigBank has a regulatory blackout from 02:30\u201303:30 PT on Sat due to overnight batch jobs; we cannot touch routes or IPs during that hour. That conflicts with the current canary window.\\n- IP whitelisting: after upgrade the sidecar metrics endpoint will originate from a new ephemeral IP range (10.200.5.0/24). Need confirmation we can add that to their VPC ACLs and firewall rules at least 24h in advance.\\n- Network diagram attached: \\\"acme_vpc_routes.png\\\" \u2014 please verify the proposed route change won't overlap the DB migration VLAN.\\n\\nIf we must move the canary earlier, we can do 00:15\u201301:15 PT for canary and bulk after the blackout, but that compresses the lead time for rollback.\\n\\nCameron\\nIntegration Lead, ACME Cloud Services\\n",
    "From: Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.ai>\\nTo: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>, Mateo Alvarez <mateo_alvarez@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>, Dylan Brooks <dylan_brooks@redwood.ai>\\nCc: Cameron Blake <cameron@acmecloud.com>\\nDate: 2027-03-22T17:46:00-07:00\\nSubject: Re: Private deployment: upgrade comms, phased rollout & rollback matrix\\n\\nCouple of compliance/controls items we'll need to bake in before sending the official notice to BigBank: \\n\\n- Audit trail: all config changes and deployment steps must be pushed to the customer's audit S3 bucket (or provided via secure share) within 2 hours of completion. Add step in runbook to capture run-level logs and signed manifests.\\n- KMS rotation: do not schedule a KMS rotation inside the 30-day soft-pin window. If BigBank wants a rotation, schedule it 48h before the upgrade or 30 days after.\\n- Evidence pack: BigBank will request pre/post snapshots and syscall-level audit logs for the canary hosts. Prepare a redacted evidence pack template we can drop into DocShare.\\n- Fallback policy: strongly prefer an automated graceful traffic shift to hosted fallback for 30\u2013120m during rollback if their infra allows it. If not possible, ensure we have a documented manual fallback and escalation path.\\n\\nI'll attach the evidence checklist to the workbook and mark the gating items.\\n\\nNeha\\nSecurity & Compliance Lead\\n",
    "From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>\\nTo: Mateo Alvarez <mateo_alvarez@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>, Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.ai>, Dylan Brooks <dylan_brooks@redwood.ai>\\nCc: Cameron Blake <cameron@acmecloud.com>, BigBank SecOps <audits@bigbank.com>\\nDate: 2027-03-23T11:05:00-07:00\\nSubject: Re: Private deployment: upgrade comms, phased rollout & rollback matrix\\n\\nThanks all \u2014 consolidated next steps below and decisions so we can lock the notice.\\n\\nDecisions: \\n- Maintenance window: Sat Mar 27 00:15\u201305:00 PT. Canary 00:15\u201301:15, blackout 02:30\u201303:30 (no route changes), bulk cutover after 03:30.\\n- Version pin: 3.3.0 soft-pin for 30 days; automatic rollback to 3.2.1 if any of the primary gates trip.\\n- Rollback approach: staged rollback (canary -> region -> full) unless critical failure; add hosted fallback as preferred option if customer consents.\\n\\nAction owners: \\n- Mateo: update matrix with canary node counts, add golden-prompt smoke tests (due 2027-03-24 12:00 PT).\\n- Karthik: finalize orchestration steps, preflight checklist, and snapshot run times (due 2027-03-24 18:00 PT).\\n- Neha: finalize evidence pack template and list of logs to push to BigBank (due 2027-03-24 15:00 PT).\\n- Dylan: publish rollback playbook with drain/blackhole commands and time estimates (due 2027-03-24 20:00 PT).\\n- Cameron / ACME: confirm IP whitelist change timing and approve route diagram (please respond by 2027-03-23 17:00 PT).\\n\\nI'll incorporate all updates into the workbook and send the customer-facing maintenance notice after we have the items above. Calendar invite + runbook link will follow.\\n\\nAttachments: upgrade_matrix_v2.xlsx, comm_plan_draft.md, acme_vpc_routes.png\\n\\nKimberly\\nSenior Program Manager, Private Deployments\\nRedwood Inference\\n"
  ],
  "title_field_name": "subject",
  "content_field_names": [
    "messages"
  ],

    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Break-glass access (RBAC v2): emergency admin procedure and controls\",\n  \"space\": \"security-and-compliance\",\n  \"author\": \"Marcus Lin\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"security\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2025-01-22\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2025-03-21\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Dr. Aisha Rahman\",\n    \"Naomi Feldman\",\n    \"Priya Natarajan\",\n    \"Fiona McCarthy\",\n    \"Kevin Osei\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"rbac-v2\",\n    \"break-glass\",\n    \"least-privilege\",\n    \"audit-logging\",\n    \"soc2\",\n    \"private-deployments\",\n    \"incident-response\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"restricted\",\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"confluence://security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth/rbac-v2-design-overview\",\n    \"confluence://security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth/rbac-v2-migration-and-backwards-compatibility\",\n    \"confluence://security-and-compliance/audit-logging/authz-decision-logging-schema\",\n    \"confluence://architecture-and-standards/api-standards/authorization-check-patterns\",\n    \"confluence://architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-014-permission-naming-and-versioning\"\n  ],\n  \"content\": \"## Overview\\nBreak-glass access is a controlled, time-bound mechanism to temporarily grant elevated privileges to resolve an incident, restore service, or perform a customer-authorized emergency operation when normal access paths (standard RBAC roles, delegated admin workflows, or automation) are insufficient.\\n\\nThis page defines:\\n- When break-glass is allowed vs prohibited\\n- The approval workflow (two-person rule) and emergency exceptions\\n- How time-bound elevation is implemented in RBAC v2\\n- Required logging, alerting, and evidence artifacts\\n- Post-use review requirements and follow-ups\\n\\nBreak-glass is designed to be compatible across **Hosted API**, **Dedicated**, and **Private** deployments, with deployment-specific operational details called out below.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Goals\\n1. **Restore or protect service quickly** during incidents while maintaining strong controls.\\n2. **Deny-by-default**: no standing \\u201csuper admin\\u201d access for day-to-day operations.\\n3. **Least privilege even in emergencies**: scoped elevation (org/project/environment/cluster) and minimal permission bundles.\\n4. **Auditability**: every request, approval, session, and privileged action is recorded with sufficient context for SOC 2 evidence and customer investigations.\\n5. **Safety**: automatic expiry, revocation on completion, and alerts on unusual behavior.\\n\\n## Non-goals\\n- Customer-configurable policy scripting (out of scope for RBAC v2).\\n- Replacing incident management processes (PagerDuty/IR remains the primary workflow).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Definitions\\n- **Break-glass request**: A formal record describing why elevated access is required.\\n- **Break-glass session**: A time-boxed grant of elevated permissions (implemented as an ephemeral RBAC binding).\\n- **Operator**: The engineer performing the emergency action.\\n- **Approver(s)**: Security/operations leaders who authorize the session.\\n- **Scoped elevation**: Session grants access only to the minimum required scope (e.g., Org A / Project B / Env prod-eu / Cluster c-17).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## When break-glass is allowed\\nBreak-glass MAY be used for:\\n- Incident response actions necessary to restore availability, integrity, or security (e.g., disable a runaway routing policy, rotate compromised keys, restore access to audit export pipeline).\\n- Emergency changes when normal admin delegation is unavailable (e.g., customer\\u2019s Security Admin is unreachable and explicit emergency authorization exists in the contract / documented escalation).\\n- Time-critical remediation of an authorization outage caused by RBAC misconfiguration or regressions.\\n\\nBreak-glass SHOULD NOT be used for:\\n- Routine administrative tasks (role assignments, policy edits, configuration changes) that can be done via standard roles.\\n- Testing, debugging convenience, or \\u201cjust to check\\u201d access.\\n- Bypassing customer change-management policies.\\n\\nBreak-glass MUST NOT be used for:\\n- Accessing customer data for curiosity, product research, or non-incident reasons.\\n- Bulk exports of customer data outside explicit incident/customer authorization.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## RBAC v2 design: how elevation works\\n### High-level approach\\nBreak-glass is implemented as a **time-bound role binding** created by the Control Plane after approval. The binding references a dedicated role template that is:\\n- narrowly permissioned (see \\u201cPermission bundles\\u201d)\\n- always explicitly scoped\\n- never assigned as a standing role\\n\\n### Entities\\n- **BreakGlassRequest** (control-plane object): requester, operator, incident/ticket reference, justification, requested scope, requested duration.\\n- **BreakGlassSession** (control-plane object): approved-by, start time, expiry, effective scopes, role template version, session ID.\\n\\n### Session duration constraints\\nDefault and maximum session lengths are enforced by the control plane:\\n- Default: **30 minutes**\\n- Maximum: **120 minutes** (requires explicit justification)\\n- Extensions: permitted only by **new approval** (no silent refresh)\\n\\n### Scoping requirements\\nBreak-glass sessions MUST specify at least one of:\\n- Org scope (org:<org_id>)\\n- Project scope (project:<project_id>)\\n- Environment scope (env:<env_id>, e.g., hosted-prod-us, dedicated-prod, private-prod)\\n- Cluster scope (cluster:<cluster_id>)\\n\\nScopes MUST be minimized. \\u201c*\\u201d scopes are not permitted for break-glass in Hosted/Dedicated production.\\n\\n### Permission bundles\\nBreak-glass sessions use one of the predefined templates below. Selection is part of approval.\\n\\n| Template | Intended use | Notes |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| BreakGlass:ControlPlaneOperator | Restore control-plane admin functions (roles, routing policy rollback, model pin rollback, key rotation) | Most common; still scoped to target org/project/env |\\n| BreakGlass:SecurityResponder | Security incident actions (revoke tokens/keys, force-rotate secrets, enable audit export, lock down org) | Requires Security approver |\\n| BreakGlass:PrivateClusterOperator | Private installer/cluster emergency operations (bootstrap admin recovery, agent connectivity, upgrade unblock) | Only available in Private deployments |\\n\\nTemplate permissions are versioned and maintained in the policy bundle repo. Any expansion of a break-glass template requires Security review and a change record.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Approval workflow (two-person rule)\\n### Standard approval path (required for production)\\nBreak-glass requires **two-person approval**:\\n1. **Approver #1 (SecOps on-call)**: validates necessity, scope, duration, and incident linkage.\\n2. **Approver #2 (Security Engineering lead or delegate)**: validates least-privilege and policy alignment.\\n\\nApprovers MUST be different individuals and MUST NOT be the operator.\\n\\n### Emergency exception (\\u201cimmediate containment\\u201d)\\nIf waiting for two approvals materially increases risk (e.g., active credential compromise, ongoing data exfiltration, platform-wide outage), a single SecOps approver may grant a **15-minute containment session** with the narrowest possible scope.\\n\\nRequirements for emergency exception:\\n- Incident must be declared in PagerDuty\\n- Second approval must be obtained retroactively within **1 business day**\\n- Post-use review is mandatory (see below)\\n\\n### Required fields on every request\\nRequests are rejected if missing:\\n- Incident/ticket reference (PagerDuty incident ID or Jira/Linear ticket)\\n- Clear justification (\\u201cwhat action will be taken\\u201d) and expected impact\\n- Explicit scope(s)\\n- Requested duration (<= 120 minutes)\\n- Operator identity (SSO user)\\n\\n### Approval checks\\nApprovers must verify:\\n- Is there a standard role/workflow that can achieve the same result? If yes, use it.\\n- Is the requested scope minimal?\\n- Is the duration minimal?\\n- Does the request involve customer data access? If yes, ensure customer authorization exists and is recorded.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Operator procedure (step-by-step)\\n### 0) Preconditions\\n- Operator must authenticate via SSO with MFA.\\n- Operator must have baseline access to initiate requests (no production admin needed).\\n\\n### 1) Create a break-glass request\\nVia Console (preferred) or CLI.\\n\\nConsole: **Security \\u2192 Break-glass \\u2192 New request**\\n\\nCLI example:\\n- `rwctl breakglass request create --org <org_id> --env hosted-prod-us --duration 30m --template ControlPlaneOperator --incident PD-12345 --reason \\\"Rollback routing policy to stop 5xx spike\\\"`\\n\\n### 2) Obtain approvals\\nApprovers review in Console and approve/deny. Approval actions are recorded in audit logs.\\n\\n### 3) Start the session\\nOnce approved, operator starts the session, which creates an ephemeral role binding:\\n- `rwctl breakglass session start --request <request_id>`\\n\\n### 4) Perform the minimal set of actions\\nOperator must:\\n- Keep changes to the minimum required for remediation\\n- Prefer reversible actions (rollback) vs novel configuration\\n- Avoid accessing customer payloads/content unless strictly required\\n\\n### 5) End session immediately after completion\\nSessions auto-expire, but operators must end sessions early:\\n- `rwctl breakglass session end --session <session_id> --note \\\"Rollback complete; error rate normalized\\\"`\\n\\n### 6) Create/attach evidence\\nOperator adds:\\n- a short summary of actions taken\\n- links to related PRs/config diffs (if applicable)\\n- relevant dashboards/log queries\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Logging requirements (auditability)\\n### Events that MUST be logged\\nThe platform MUST emit audit events for:\\n- BreakGlassRequestCreated\\n- BreakGlassRequestApproved / BreakGlassRequestDenied (with approver identity)\\n- BreakGlassSessionStarted\\n- BreakGlassSessionExtended (new approval required)\\n- BreakGlassSessionEnded\\n- BreakGlassSessionExpired\\n\\nAdditionally, all privileged actions performed during an active session MUST include authz decision context (see audit schema page), including:\\n- subject (user + org)\\n- action (permission)\\n- resource scope (org/project/env/cluster)\\n- decision (allow/deny)\\n- policy version / role template version\\n- session_id (break-glass correlation)\\n- denial_reason_code (when applicable)\\n\\n### Minimum fields for requests/sessions\\n- request_id, session_id\\n- operator_user_id, operator_email\\n- approver_user_ids (one or two)\\n- incident_id / ticket_id\\n- justification text\\n- requested_scopes + effective_scopes\\n- start_time, expiry_time, end_time\\n\\n### Retention and export\\n- Audit logs containing break-glass activity are classified as **security-relevant** and follow the standard retention policy for security events.\\n- For enterprise accounts, audit export to SIEM MUST include the break-glass fields and session correlation identifiers.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Alerting and monitoring requirements\\n### Real-time alerts\\nThe system MUST alert on:\\n- Session started in production environments\\n- Session extension request\\n- Any use of SecurityResponder template\\n- Any attempt to create a request with overly broad scope (should be rejected; alert if attempted)\\n\\nAlerts go to:\\n- Slack: **#secops** and **#eng-platform-oncall**\\n- PagerDuty: **SecOps on-call** (high priority for SecurityResponder)\\n\\n### Anomaly monitoring (daily)\\nSecurity Engineering reviews daily detections:\\n- Multiple break-glass sessions by same operator in 24h\\n- Break-glass use without a linked incident\\n- High volume of privileged actions during a session\\n- Access patterns inconsistent with request justification (manual triage)\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Post-use review (mandatory)\\n### Timeline\\nA post-use review MUST be completed within:\\n- **24 hours** for emergency exception sessions\\n- **3 business days** for standard sessions\\n\\n### Reviewer(s)\\n- Security Engineering (owner)\\n- SecOps (operational validation)\\n- Platform on-call (if platform-impacting)\\n\\n### Review checklist\\n1. Was break-glass necessary vs standard role/workflow?\\n2. Was scope minimal and correct?\\n3. Was duration minimal? Was session ended promptly?\\n4. Were actions consistent with stated justification?\\n5. Were any customer payloads/content accessed? If yes:\\n   - was it required?\\n   - is customer notification required per contract/policy?\\n6. Do we need follow-ups?\\n   - create/adjust role templates to avoid future break-glass\\n   - add tests/guardrails\\n   - update runbooks/docs\\n\\n### Required artifacts (evidence-ready)\\nAttach to the incident/ticket:\\n- Request + session IDs\\n- Audit log query link showing session start/end and key actions\\n- Summary of actions taken and outcome\\n- Approver identities and timestamps\\n- Any corrective actions (PRs, role template changes, regression tests)\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Deployment-specific notes\\n### Hosted API / Dedicated\\n- \\u201c*\\u201d scope break-glass is disallowed in production.\\n- Break-glass sessions are created via the central control plane and enforced by the gateway + service interceptors.\\n- If authz services are degraded, the platform follows the fail-closed policy; break-glass is not a bypass of authentication/authorization enforcement, it is a controlled way to grant permissions.\\n\\n### Private deployments\\nPrivate has additional realities (customer networking, restricted egress):\\n- Break-glass sessions still require the same approval semantics, but approvals may be executed by the customer\\u2019s designated Security Admin if the deployment is configured for customer-controlled operations.\\n- If the private control plane cannot reach Redwood systems, audit logs must spool locally and be exportable once connectivity resumes.\\n- Installer bootstrap recovery uses the **PrivateClusterOperator** template and is always cluster-scoped.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Controls and safeguards\\n- **MFA required** for all break-glass operators and approvers.\\n- **No shared accounts**; sessions are tied to a human identity.\\n- **Time-bound binding** with hard expiry enforced server-side.\\n- **No silent extensions**; extensions require approval and are separately logged.\\n- **Deny-by-default enforcement** remains in place; break-glass grants permissions, it does not disable checks.\\n- **Separation of duties**: operator cannot self-approve.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Frequently asked questions\\n### Why not keep standing \\u201csuper admin\\u201d roles?\\nStanding access increases the blast radius of credential compromise and makes least-privilege evidence difficult. Break-glass provides a controlled mechanism that is explicitly logged, time-bound, and scoped.\\n\\n### Does break-glass bypass authorization checks?\\nNo. It creates a temporary, auditable authorization grant. All permission checks remain enforced by the gateway/services.\\n\\n### What if break-glass is needed because RBAC itself is broken?\\nIf RBAC enforcement is malfunctioning, the incident is treated as a security and availability event. Use the emergency exception for minimal containment actions, prioritize rollback/feature-flag disablement, and ensure full post-use review.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Ownership\\n- Policy + implementation: **Security Engineering** (Marcus Lin)\\n- Alerting + on-call approvals: **SecOps** (Fiona McCarthy)\\n- Audit log schema + SIEM export: **Audit Logging** (Kevin Osei)\\n\\nFor changes to templates/permissions or approval rules, open a Security change request and link to the relevant ADR/PR.\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"content\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_99c5a8ae5124458ea4cc4345b47a351f\"\n}",

{
  "title": "Break-glass access (RBAC v2): emergency admin procedure and controls",
  "space": "security-and-compliance",
  "author": "Marcus Lin",
  "owner_team": "security",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2025-01-22",
  "last_updated": "2025-03-21",
  "reviewers": [
    "Dr. Aisha Rahman",
    "Naomi Feldman",
    "Priya Natarajan",
    "Fiona McCarthy",
    "Kevin Osei"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "rbac-v2",
    "break-glass",
    "least-privilege",
    "audit-logging",
    "soc2",
    "private-deployments",
    "incident-response"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "restricted",
  "related_pages": [
    "confluence://security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth/rbac-v2-design-overview",
    "confluence://security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth/rbac-v2-migration-and-backwards-compatibility",
    "confluence://security-and-compliance/audit-logging/authz-decision-logging-schema",
    "confluence://architecture-and-standards/api-standards/authorization-check-patterns",
    "confluence://architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-014-permission-naming-and-versioning"
  ],
  "content": "## Overview
Break-glass access is a controlled, time-bound mechanism to temporarily grant elevated privileges to resolve an incident, restore service, or perform a customer-authorized emergency operation when normal access paths (standard RBAC roles, delegated admin workflows, or automation) are insufficient.

This page defines:
- When break-glass is allowed vs prohibited
- The approval workflow (two-person rule) and emergency exceptions
- How time-bound elevation is implemented in RBAC v2
- Required logging, alerting, and evidence artifacts
- Post-use review requirements and follow-ups

Break-glass is designed to be compatible across **Hosted API**, **Dedicated**, and **Private** deployments, with deployment-specific operational details called out below.

---

## Goals
1. **Restore or protect service quickly** during incidents while maintaining strong controls.
2. **Deny-by-default**: no standing “super admin” access for day-to-day operations.
3. **Least privilege even in emergencies**: scoped elevation (org/project/environment/cluster) and minimal permission bundles.
4. **Auditability**: every request, approval, session, and privileged action is recorded with sufficient context for SOC 2 evidence and customer investigations.
5. **Safety**: automatic expiry, revocation on completion, and alerts on unusual behavior.

## Non-goals
- Customer-configurable policy scripting (out of scope for RBAC v2).
- Replacing incident management processes (PagerDuty/IR remains the primary workflow).

---

## Definitions
- **Break-glass request**: A formal record describing why elevated access is required.
- **Break-glass session**: A time-boxed grant of elevated permissions (implemented as an ephemeral RBAC binding).
- **Operator**: The engineer performing the emergency action.
- **Approver(s)**: Security/operations leaders who authorize the session.
- **Scoped elevation**: Session grants access only to the minimum required scope (e.g., Org A / Project B / Env prod-eu / Cluster c-17).

---

## When break-glass is allowed
Break-glass MAY be used for:
- Incident response actions necessary to restore availability, integrity, or security (e.g., disable a runaway routing policy, rotate compromised keys, restore access to audit export pipeline).
- Emergency changes when normal admin delegation is unavailable (e.g., customer’s Security Admin is unreachable and explicit emergency authorization exists in the contract / documented escalation).
- Time-critical remediation of an authorization outage caused by RBAC misconfiguration or regressions.

Break-glass SHOULD NOT be used for:
- Routine administrative tasks (role assignments, policy edits, configuration changes) that can be done via standard roles.
- Testing, debugging convenience, or “just to check” access.
- Bypassing customer change-management policies.

Break-glass MUST NOT be used for:
- Accessing customer data for curiosity, product research, or non-incident reasons.
- Bulk exports of customer data outside explicit incident/customer authorization.

---

## RBAC v2 design: how elevation works
### High-level approach
Break-glass is implemented as a **time-bound role binding** created by the Control Plane after approval. The binding references a dedicated role template that is:
- narrowly permissioned (see “Permission bundles”)
- always explicitly scoped
- never assigned as a standing role

### Entities
- **BreakGlassRequest** (control-plane object): requester, operator, incident/ticket reference, justification, requested scope, requested duration.
- **BreakGlassSession** (control-plane object): approved-by, start time, expiry, effective scopes, role template version, session ID.

### Session duration constraints
Default and maximum session lengths are enforced by the control plane:
- Default: **30 minutes**
- Maximum: **120 minutes** (requires explicit justification)
- Extensions: permitted only by **new approval** (no silent refresh)

### Scoping requirements
Break-glass sessions MUST specify at least one of:
- Org scope (org:<org_id>)
- Project scope (project:<project_id>)
- Environment scope (env:<env_id>, e.g., hosted-prod-us, dedicated-prod, private-prod)
- Cluster scope (cluster:<cluster_id>)

Scopes MUST be minimized. “*” scopes are not permitted for break-glass in Hosted/Dedicated production.

### Permission bundles
Break-glass sessions use one of the predefined templates below. Selection is part of approval.

| Template | Intended use | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| BreakGlass:ControlPlaneOperator | Restore control-plane admin functions (roles, routing policy rollback, model pin rollback, key rotation) | Most common; still scoped to target org/project/env |
| BreakGlass:SecurityResponder | Security incident actions (revoke tokens/keys, force-rotate secrets, enable audit export, lock down org) | Requires Security approver |
| BreakGlass:PrivateClusterOperator | Private installer/cluster emergency operations (bootstrap admin recovery, agent connectivity, upgrade unblock) | Only available in Private deployments |

Template permissions are versioned and maintained in the policy bundle repo. Any expansion of a break-glass template requires Security review and a change record.

---

## Approval workflow (two-person rule)
### Standard approval path (required for production)
Break-glass requires **two-person approval**:
1. **Approver #1 (SecOps on-call)**: validates necessity, scope, duration, and incident linkage.
2. **Approver #2 (Security Engineering lead or delegate)**: validates least-privilege and policy alignment.

Approvers MUST be different individuals and MUST NOT be the operator.

### Emergency exception (“immediate containment”)
If waiting for two approvals materially increases risk (e.g., active credential compromise, ongoing data exfiltration, platform-wide outage), a single SecOps approver may grant a **15-minute containment session** with the narrowest possible scope.

Requirements for emergency exception:
- Incident must be declared in PagerDuty
- Second approval must be obtained retroactively within **1 business day**
- Post-use review is mandatory (see below)

### Required fields on every request
Requests are rejected if missing:
- Incident/ticket reference (PagerDuty incident ID or Jira/Linear ticket)
- Clear justification (“what action will be taken”) and expected impact
- Explicit scope(s)
- Requested duration (<= 120 minutes)
- Operator identity (SSO user)

### Approval checks
Approvers must verify:
- Is there a standard role/workflow that can achieve the same result? If yes, use it.
- Is the requested scope minimal?
- Is the duration minimal?
- Does the request involve customer data access? If yes, ensure customer authorization exists and is recorded.

---

## Operator procedure (step-by-step)
### 0) Preconditions
- Operator must authenticate via SSO with MFA.
- Operator must have baseline access to initiate requests (no production admin needed).

### 1) Create a break-glass request
Via Console (preferred) or CLI.

Console: **Security → Break-glass → New request**

CLI example:
- `rwctl breakglass request create --org <org_id> --env hosted-prod-us --duration 30m --template ControlPlaneOperator --incident PD-12345 --reason "Rollback routing policy to stop 5xx spike"`

### 2) Obtain approvals
Approvers review in Console and approve/deny. Approval actions are recorded in audit logs.

### 3) Start the session
Once approved, operator starts the session, which creates an ephemeral role binding:
- `rwctl breakglass session start --request <request_id>`

### 4) Perform the minimal set of actions
Operator must:
- Keep changes to the minimum required for remediation
- Prefer reversible actions (rollback) vs novel configuration
- Avoid accessing customer payloads/content unless strictly required

### 5) End session immediately after completion
Sessions auto-expire, but operators must end sessions early:
- `rwctl breakglass session end --session <session_id> --note "Rollback complete; error rate normalized"`

### 6) Create/attach evidence
Operator adds:
- a short summary of actions taken
- links to related PRs/config diffs (if applicable)
- relevant dashboards/log queries

---

## Logging requirements (auditability)
### Events that MUST be logged
The platform MUST emit audit events for:
- BreakGlassRequestCreated
- BreakGlassRequestApproved / BreakGlassRequestDenied (with approver identity)
- BreakGlassSessionStarted
- BreakGlassSessionExtended (new approval required)
- BreakGlassSessionEnded
- BreakGlassSessionExpired

Additionally, all privileged actions performed during an active session MUST include authz decision context (see audit schema page), including:
- subject (user + org)
- action (permission)
- resource scope (org/project/env/cluster)
- decision (allow/deny)
- policy version / role template version
- session_id (break-glass correlation)
- denial_reason_code (when applicable)

### Minimum fields for requests/sessions
- request_id, session_id
- operator_user_id, operator_email
- approver_user_ids (one or two)
- incident_id / ticket_id
- justification text
- requested_scopes + effective_scopes
- start_time, expiry_time, end_time

### Retention and export
- Audit logs containing break-glass activity are classified as **security-relevant** and follow the standard retention policy for security events.
- For enterprise accounts, audit export to SIEM MUST include the break-glass fields and session correlation identifiers.

---

## Alerting and monitoring requirements
### Real-time alerts
The system MUST alert on:
- Session started in production environments
- Session extension request
- Any use of SecurityResponder template
- Any attempt to create a request with overly broad scope (should be rejected; alert if attempted)

Alerts go to:
- Slack: **#secops** and **#eng-platform-oncall**
- PagerDuty: **SecOps on-call** (high priority for SecurityResponder)

### Anomaly monitoring (daily)
Security Engineering reviews daily detections:
- Multiple break-glass sessions by same operator in 24h
- Break-glass use without a linked incident
- High volume of privileged actions during a session
- Access patterns inconsistent with request justification (manual triage)

---

## Post-use review (mandatory)
### Timeline
A post-use review MUST be completed within:
- **24 hours** for emergency exception sessions
- **3 business days** for standard sessions

### Reviewer(s)
- Security Engineering (owner)
- SecOps (operational validation)
- Platform on-call (if platform-impacting)

### Review checklist
1. Was break-glass necessary vs standard role/workflow?
2. Was scope minimal and correct?
3. Was duration minimal? Was session ended promptly?
4. Were actions consistent with stated justification?
5. Were any customer payloads/content accessed? If yes:
   - was it required?
   - is customer notification required per contract/policy?
6. Do we need follow-ups?
   - create/adjust role templates to avoid future break-glass
   - add tests/guardrails
   - update runbooks/docs

### Required artifacts (evidence-ready)
Attach to the incident/ticket:
- Request + session IDs
- Audit log query link showing session start/end and key actions
- Summary of actions taken and outcome
- Approver identities and timestamps
- Any corrective actions (PRs, role template changes, regression tests)

---

## Deployment-specific notes
### Hosted API / Dedicated
- “*” scope break-glass is disallowed in production.
- Break-glass sessions are created via the central control plane and enforced by the gateway + service interceptors.
- If authz services are degraded, the platform follows the fail-closed policy; break-glass is not a bypass of authentication/authorization enforcement, it is a controlled way to grant permissions.

### Private deployments
Private has additional realities (customer networking, restricted egress):
- Break-glass sessions still require the same approval semantics, but approvals may be executed by the customer’s designated Security Admin if the deployment is configured for customer-controlled operations.
- If the private control plane cannot reach Redwood systems, audit logs must spool locally and be exportable once connectivity resumes.
- Installer bootstrap recovery uses the **PrivateClusterOperator** template and is always cluster-scoped.

---

## Controls and safeguards
- **MFA required** for all break-glass operators and approvers.
- **No shared accounts**; sessions are tied to a human identity.
- **Time-bound binding** with hard expiry enforced server-side.
- **No silent extensions**; extensions require approval and are separately logged.
- **Deny-by-default enforcement** remains in place; break-glass grants permissions, it does not disable checks.
- **Separation of duties**: operator cannot self-approve.

---

## Frequently asked questions
### Why not keep standing “super admin” roles?
Standing access increases the blast radius of credential compromise and makes least-privilege evidence difficult. Break-glass provides a controlled mechanism that is explicitly logged, time-bound, and scoped.

### Does break-glass bypass authorization checks?
No. It creates a temporary, auditable authorization grant. All permission checks remain enforced by the gateway/services.

### What if break-glass is needed because RBAC itself is broken?
If RBAC enforcement is malfunctioning, the incident is treated as a security and availability event. Use the emergency exception for minimal containment actions, prioritize rollback/feature-flag disablement, and ensure full post-use review.

---

## Ownership
- Policy + implementation: **Security Engineering** (Marcus Lin)
- Alerting + on-call approvals: **SecOps** (Fiona McCarthy)
- Audit log schema + SIEM export: **Audit Logging** (Kevin Osei)

For changes to templates/permissions or approval rules, open a Security change request and link to the relevant ADR/PR.

    "title": "Incremental Snapshot Retention and Rollback Guidance for Private Deployments",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/google_drive",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Incremental Snapshot Retention and Rollback Guidance for Private Deployments\",\n  \"owner\": \"Priya Iyer\",\n  \"drive_area\": \"shared_drives\",\n  \"path\": \"shared_drives/engineering/private-deployments/incremental-snapshot-retention-and-rollback-guidance\",\n  \"doc_type\": \"doc\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2024-11-03\",\n  \"last_modified\": \"2026-03-06\",\n  \"collaborators\": [\n    \"Marcus Lee\",\n    \"Sofia Alvarez\",\n    \"Daniel Cho\"\n  ],\n  \"team\": \"eng-private-deployments\",\n  \"status\": \"in_review\",\n  \"tags\": [\n    \"disaster-recovery\",\n    \"snapshots\",\n    \"terraform\",\n    \"on-prem\",\n    \"backup\",\n    \"retention\",\n    \"playbook\"\n  ],\n  \"linked_artifacts\": [\n    \"CONFLUENCE-DR-PLAN-981\",\n    \"JIRA-PRIV-4321\",\n    \"https://github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-private-deployments/pull/218\"\n  ],\n  \"body\": \"Purpose and scope:\\\\n\\\\nThis doc is a working draft describing an incremental snapshot retention policy and a stepwise rollback/restore guidance for Redwood Private deployments (VPC and on-prem packages). It focuses on:\\\\n- safe incremental backups for disks/object stores,\\\\n- consistent restore points across services (control plane DB, model artifacts, KV caches, infrastructure config),\\\\n- Terraform state and module considerations for restore after failure or as part of upgrade rollback, and\\\\n- verification steps and test plans for DR rehearsals.\\\\n\\\\nAudience:\\\\nPrimary: platform engineers, SRE, and solutions engineers who run customer private deployments. Secondary: product security and support on-call.\\\\n\\\\nHigh-level RTO/RPO targets (proposal):\\\\n- Control plane metadata DB (Postgres): RTO 30m, RPO 15m (via WAL shipping / streaming replication + incremental snapshots)\\\\n- Model artifacts (object store): RTO 2h, RPO 1h (incremental object layer + manifest versioning)\\\\n- Serving runtime (GPU state + cache): RTO best-effort (repopulate caches), RPO N/A (caches reconstructed)\\\\n- Terraform state: RTO 1h, RPO ideally 0 (state stored in a versioned backend - see notes)\\\\n\\\\nSnapshot strategy overview:\\\\n1) Multi-layer snapshots:\\\\n   - Block-level incremental snapshots for instance volumes (EBS/ZFS/CEPH) every 30 minutes for critical nodes (control plane), hourly for compute nodes.\\\\n   - Object-store incremental syncs (rsync/rclone/replication to S3-compatible backend) for model artifacts every 15 minutes for active training/ingest clusters, hourly otherwise.\\\\n   - Logical DB backups: base backup nightly + WAL segments retained for 7 days (configured via retention window) and shipped to cold storage.\\\\n\\\\n2) Consistency windows and application quiesce:\\\\n   - For a point-in-time consistent restore across multiple resources, create a coordinated checkpoint: pause writes to the control plane APIs, flush DB WAL, snapshot volumes, then resume. This is required for production-grade consistency; for best RTO tradeoffs, use asynchronous replication with known divergence bounds.\\\\n\\\\n3) Retention policy (recommended starting point):\\\\n   - Short-term retention: keep all incremental snapshots for the last 72 hours.\\\\n   - Mid-term retention: keep hourly consolidated deltas for 7 days.\\\\n   - Long-term retention: keep daily consolidated full snapshot (or manifest) for 90 days.\\\\n   - Archive: weekly full snapshot stored in cold object store for 1 year for compliance customers.\\\\n\\\\nTerraform-specific notes (modules and state):\\\\n- State backend: always use a versioned, tamper-evident backend (e.g., remote backend with object-versioning + server-side encryption + write-once lifecycle for older state snapshots) for terraform.tfstate. For airgapped/offline installs, we maintain an encrypted state artifact pushed to the customer's S3-compatible archive and to a vendor-side store for recovery.\\\\n- Module design considerations: keep infrastructure bootstrap modules idempotent and small. Do not place long-lived, mutable customer data in a module; reference it via data sources.\\\\n- Recovery path for corrupted state: follow recovery steps in the terraform/README for the private-deploy repo: retrieve last known-good state artifact, run terraform init with the recovered backend, plan to detect drift, then terraform apply in a controlled maintenance window.\\\\n- Important modules to track for DR: module.network (VPC/subnet routing), module.storage (object store configuration), module.db (managed Postgres/primary replicas), module.k8s (cluster config). Add a module-level tag `dr-critical` to resources that must be restored before application traffic resumes.\\\\n\\\\nRollback/restore playbook (tagged, actionable steps)\\\\n- Goal: recover to a chosen snapshot point with minimal manual intervention. The numbered steps assume control-plane operator access and an approved incident ticket.\\\\n\\\\n1) Triage and decision:\\\\n   - Confirm incident scope (single node, region, or full cluster). Attach telemetry: instance health, recent deployment PRs, terraform changes, and storage IO errors.\\\\n   - If data corruption suspected, select a point-in-time earlier than the suspected window. For software regressions, consider rolling forward to a patched build if faster than restore.\\\\n\\\\n2) Prepare recovery environment:\\\\n   - Create an incident branch in terraform (name: incident/YYYYMMDD/owner) to avoid accidental changes to main.\\\\n   - Lock the terraform state backend (if supported) to prevent concurrent writes.\\\\n   - If on-prem airgapped: provision a recovery host with access to the snapshot archive (USB/NAS import or S3-compatible endpoint).\\\\n\\\\n3) Retrieve and validate snapshots:\\\\n   - Fetch the control-plane DB base backup + relevant WAL segments. Validate checksums (we store SHA256 in the snapshot manifest).\\\\n   - For object artifacts: download manifest and a sample of files to validate content and sizes.\\\\n   - Validate terraform state artifact integrity against the artifact manifest (pgp/gpg signature where available).\\\\n\\\\n4) Restore sequence (order matters):\\\\n   - Restore network and storage primitives first (VPC routes, object store buckets, volume attachments). Many resources must exist before databases and control-plane services can mount.\\\\n   - Restore DB base backup and replay WAL to the chosen point. Start DB in single-user recovery mode and run smoke SQL tests.\\\\n   - Restore control-plane application metadata (if separate from DB) and run migration rollbacks (if necessary).\\\\n   - Rehydrate model artifacts to object store and validate manifests. For large artifact sets, use concurrent multipart uploads and validate ETags.\\\\n   - Bring up control-plane services with maintenance mode enabled. Wait for health checks and read-only queries to succeed.\\\\n   - Verify telemetry (API responses, example request paths, canary inference) before enabling write traffic.\\\\n\\\\n5) Terraform state reconciliation:\\\\n   - After infrastructure is present, run terraform plan against recovered state to detect drift. Carefully review plan; for destructive changes, require a second approver.\\\\n   - Apply only the minimal set of changes necessary to restore resource attachments (e.g., volume attachments) unless a full reapply was planned.\\\\n\\\\n6) Post-restore validation and smoke tests:\\\\n   - Run end-to-end canaries: token-level inference on a pinned model, model artifact checksums, session restore, and a synthetic high-load test at reduced concurrency.\\\\n   - Validate billing/usage counters and token accounting sanity for the recovered window.\\\\n\\\\n7) Communication and closeout:\\\\n   - Update incident ticket with timeline, chosen snapshot id(s), and root cause hypothesis.\\\\n   - Schedule a postmortem and DR rehearsal if the restore was > 1 hour or if recovery revealed process gaps.\\\\n\\\\nEdge cases and notes:\\\\n- Partial corruption of model artifacts: support repair by re-fetching artifacts from upstream model registry. Maintain a canonical model manifest in a separate versioned store to allow selective re-download.\\\\n- Long-running WAL gaps: if WAL segments are missing, we may have to restore to the last complete base backup. Document the data loss window explicitly and notify stakeholders.\\\\n- Terraform drift vs config rollback: if the incident is a bad terraform change, prefer a state-driven rollback using the last-good state artifact rather than reapplying the bad config. Keep a copy of the PR that triggered the change in linked_artifacts.\\\\n\\\\nTest plan for DR rehearsals (quarterly recommended):\\\\n- Smoke rehearsal (monthly): restore DB to a test namespace, run the canary suite. Validate RTO < 1 hour for control-plane-only restores.\\\\n- Partial restore (quarterly): restore object-store artifacts for one model and validate serving.\\\\n- Full rehearse (biannual): in a non-production region or isolated customer env, perform full coordinated checkpoint and restore to prove end-to-end recovery. Capture timings for RTO/RPO metrics.\\\\n\\\\nTerraform helper snippets (notes for module maintainers):\\\\n- Store tfstate with object versioning enabled. Tag state snapshots with incident metadata: {\\\"incident_id\\\": \\\"JIRA-PRIV-4321\\\", \\\"snapshot_point\\\": \\\"2026-03-05T03:00Z\\\"}.\\\\n- Add lifecycle rules to important resources to prevent accidental deletion: lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } behind a feature flag.\\\\n- Export a `dr_snapshot_manifest` from the infra bootstrap to central archive (manifest includes SHA256 checksums, creation timestamp, list of snapshots and terraform state id).\\\\n\\\\nOpen questions / TODOs (working list):\\\\n- Decide default retention SLAs for enterprise vs self-hosted customers (pricing implications).\\\\n- Add automated manifest signing for object snapshots (GPG/PGP) and wire a verification step into our restore automation.\\\\n- Define small-footprint recovery tooling for completely airgapped installs (USB import tooling, encrypted keys rotation).\\\\n- Integrate a restore dry-run in the CI for terraform modules to ensure idempotency on a test backend.\\\\n\\\\nAppendix: quick command references (examples, operator scratchpad)\\\\n- List snapshots (example): psnapctl list --cluster-id $CLUSTER --since 72h\\\\n- Download manifest: rclone copy s3:customer-archive/$CLUSTER/manifests/$SNAPSHOT.json ./\\\\n- Verify checksum: sha256sum -c ./snapshot.manifest.sha256\\\\n- Postgres restore skeleton: pg_basebackup -D /var/lib/postgres/data -R -X fetch -z --verbose --label=\\\\\\\"$SNAP_ID\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\nNotes to self / rough TODOs:\\\\n- Convert this draft into a short runbook with 1-page quick start, then a detailed appendix for engineers.\\\\n- Pair with security on key management for archived states.\\\\n- Add a simple terraform module test harness for simulated state recoveries.\\\\n\\\\nEnd of draft.\\\\n\\\\n(Informal notes: lots of shorthand above, need to add specific customer examples and map to on-prem storage vendors like NetApp/CEPH, and to cloud object stores for hybrid installs. Also follow up with Marcus on the WAL retention economics spreadsheet - JIRA-PRIV-4321.)\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_67fd0fa35c704bcbac0e7aa23fcd6285\"\n}",

document.content:
{
  "title": "Incremental Snapshot Retention and Rollback Guidance for Private Deployments",
  "owner": "Priya Iyer",
  "drive_area": "shared_drives",
  "path": "shared_drives/engineering/private-deployments/incremental-snapshot-retention-and-rollback-guidance",
  "doc_type": "doc",
  "created_at": "2024-11-03",
  "last_modified": "2026-03-06",
  "collaborators": [
    "Marcus Lee",
    "Sofia Alvarez",
    "Daniel Cho"
  ],
  "team": "eng-private-deployments",
  "status": "in_review",
  "tags": [
    "disaster-recovery",
    "snapshots",
    "terraform",
    "on-prem",
    "backup",
    "retention",
    "playbook"
  ],
  "linked_artifacts": [
    "CONFLUENCE-DR-PLAN-981",
    "JIRA-PRIV-4321",
    "https://github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-private-deployments/pull/218"
  ],
  "body": "Purpose and scope:\\n\\nThis doc is a working draft describing an incremental snapshot retention policy and a stepwise rollback/restore guidance for Redwood Private deployments (VPC and on-prem packages). It focuses on:\\n- safe incremental backups for disks/object stores,\\n- consistent restore points across services (control plane DB, model artifacts, KV caches, infrastructure config),\\n- Terraform state and module considerations for restore after failure or as part of upgrade rollback, and\\n- verification steps and test plans for DR rehearsals.\\n\\nAudience:\\nPrimary: platform engineers, SRE, and solutions engineers who run customer private deployments. Secondary: product security and support on-call.\\n\\nHigh-level RTO/RPO targets (proposal):\\n- Control plane metadata DB (Postgres): RTO 30m, RPO 15m (via WAL shipping / streaming replication + incremental snapshots)\\n- Model artifacts (object store): RTO 2h, RPO 1h (incremental object layer + manifest versioning)\\n- Serving runtime (GPU state + cache): RTO best-effort (repopulate caches), RPO N/A (caches reconstructed)\\n- Terraform state: RTO 1h, RPO ideally 0 (state stored in a versioned backend - see notes)\\n\\nSnapshot strategy overview:\\n1) Multi-layer snapshots:\\n   - Block-level incremental snapshots for instance volumes (EBS/ZFS/CEPH) every 30 minutes for critical nodes (control plane), hourly for compute nodes.\\n   - Object-store incremental syncs (rsync/rclone/replication to S3-compatible backend) for model artifacts every 15 minutes for active training/ingest clusters, hourly otherwise.\\n   - Logical DB backups: base backup nightly + WAL segments retained for 7 days (configured via retention window) and shipped to cold storage.\\n\\n2) Consistency windows and application quiesce:\\n   - For a point-in-time consistent restore across multiple resources, create a coordinated checkpoint: pause writes to the control plane APIs, flush DB WAL, snapshot volumes, then resume. This is required for production-grade consistency; for best RTO tradeoffs, use asynchronous replication with known divergence bounds.\\n\\n3) Retention policy (recommended starting point):\\n   - Short-term retention: keep all incremental snapshots for the last 72 hours.\\n   - Mid-term retention: keep hourly consolidated deltas for 7 days.\\n   - Long-term retention: keep daily consolidated full snapshot (or manifest) for 90 days.\\n   - Archive: weekly full snapshot stored in cold object store for 1 year for compliance customers.\\n\\nTerraform-specific notes (modules and state):\\n- State backend: always use a versioned, tamper-evident backend (e.g., remote backend with object-versioning + server-side encryption + write-once lifecycle for older state snapshots) for terraform.tfstate. For airgapped/offline installs, we maintain an encrypted state artifact pushed to the customer's S3-compatible archive and to a vendor-side store for recovery.\\n- Module design considerations: keep infrastructure bootstrap modules idempotent and small. Do not place long-lived, mutable customer data in a module; reference it via data sources.\\n- Recovery path for corrupted state: follow recovery steps in the terraform/README for the private-deploy repo: retrieve last known-good state artifact, run terraform init with the recovered backend, plan to detect drift, then terraform apply in a controlled maintenance window.\\n- Important modules to track for DR: module.network (VPC/subnet routing), module.storage (object store configuration), module.db (managed Postgres/primary replicas), module.k8s (cluster config). Add a module-level tag `dr-critical` to resources that must be restored before application traffic resumes.\\n\\nRollback/restore playbook (tagged, actionable steps)\\n- Goal: recover to a chosen snapshot point with minimal manual intervention. The numbered steps assume control-plane operator access and an approved incident ticket.\\n\\n1) Triage and decision:\\n   - Confirm incident scope (single node, region, or full cluster). Attach telemetry: instance health, recent deployment PRs, terraform changes, and storage IO errors.\\n   - If data corruption suspected, select a point-in-time earlier than the suspected window. For software regressions, consider rolling forward to a patched build if faster than restore.\\n\\n2) Prepare recovery environment:\\n   - Create an incident branch in terraform (name: incident/YYYYMMDD/owner) to avoid accidental changes to main.\\n   - Lock the terraform state backend (if supported) to prevent concurrent writes.\\n   - If on-prem airgapped: provision a recovery host with access to the snapshot archive (USB/NAS import or S3-compatible endpoint).\\n\\n3) Retrieve and validate snapshots:\\n   - Fetch the control-plane DB base backup + relevant WAL segments. Validate checksums (we store SHA256 in the snapshot manifest).\\n   - For object artifacts: download manifest and a sample of files to validate content and sizes.\\n   - Validate terraform state artifact integrity against the artifact manifest (pgp/gpg signature where available).\\n\\n4) Restore sequence (order matters):\\n   - Restore network and storage primitives first (VPC routes, object store buckets, volume attachments). Many resources must exist before databases and control-plane services can mount.\\n   - Restore DB base backup and replay WAL to the chosen point. Start DB in single-user recovery mode and run smoke SQL tests.\\n   - Restore control-plane application metadata (if separate from DB) and run migration rollbacks (if necessary).\\n   - Rehydrate model artifacts to object store and validate manifests. For large artifact sets, use concurrent multipart uploads and validate ETags.\\n   - Bring up control-plane services with maintenance mode enabled. Wait for health checks and read-only queries to succeed.\\n   - Verify telemetry (API responses, example request paths, canary inference) before enabling write traffic.\\n\\n5) Terraform state reconciliation:\\n   - After infrastructure is present, run terraform plan against recovered state to detect drift. Carefully review plan; for destructive changes, require a second approver.\\n   - Apply only the minimal set of changes necessary to restore resource attachments (e.g., volume attachments) unless a full reapply was planned.\\n\\n6) Post-restore validation and smoke tests:\\n   - Run end-to-end canaries: token-level inference on a pinned model, model artifact checksums, session restore, and a synthetic high-load test at reduced concurrency.\\n   - Validate billing/usage counters and token accounting sanity for the recovered window.\\n\\n7) Communication and closeout:\\n   - Update incident ticket with timeline, chosen snapshot id(s), and root cause hypothesis.\\n   - Schedule a postmortem and DR rehearsal if the restore was > 1 hour or if recovery revealed process gaps.\\n\\nEdge cases and notes:\\n- Partial corruption of model artifacts: support repair by re-fetching artifacts from upstream model registry. Maintain a canonical model manifest in a separate versioned store to allow selective re-download.\\n- Long-running WAL gaps: if WAL segments are missing, we may have to restore to the last complete base backup. Document the data loss window explicitly and notify stakeholders.\\n- Terraform drift vs config rollback: if the incident is a bad terraform change, prefer a state-driven rollback using the last-good state artifact rather than reapplying the bad config. Keep a copy of the PR that triggered the change in linked_artifacts.\\n\\nTest plan for DR rehearsals (quarterly recommended):\\n- Smoke rehearsal (monthly): restore DB to a test namespace, run the canary suite. Validate RTO < 1 hour for control-plane-only restores.\\n- Partial restore (quarterly): restore object-store artifacts for one model and validate serving.\\n- Full rehearse (biannual): in a non-production region or isolated customer env, perform full coordinated checkpoint and restore to prove end-to-end recovery. Capture timings for RTO/RPO metrics.\\n\\nTerraform helper snippets (notes for module maintainers):\\n- Store tfstate with object versioning enabled. Tag state snapshots with incident metadata: {\"incident_id\": \"JIRA-PRIV-4321\", \"snapshot_point\": \"2026-03-05T03:00Z\"}.\\n- Add lifecycle rules to important resources to prevent accidental deletion: lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } behind a feature flag.\\n- Export a `dr_snapshot_manifest` from the infra bootstrap to central archive (manifest includes SHA256 checksums, creation timestamp, list of snapshots and terraform state id).\\n\\nOpen questions / TODOs (working list):\\n- Decide default retention SLAs for enterprise vs self-hosted customers (pricing implications).\\n- Add automated manifest signing for object snapshots (GPG/PGP) and wire a verification step into our restore automation.\\n- Define small-footprint recovery tooling for completely airgapped installs (USB import tooling, encrypted keys rotation).\\n- Integrate a restore dry-run in the CI for terraform modules to ensure idempotency on a test backend.\\n\\nAppendix: quick command references (examples, operator scratchpad)\\n- List snapshots (example): psnapctl list --cluster-id $CLUSTER --since 72h\\n- Download manifest: rclone copy s3:customer-archive/$CLUSTER/manifests/$SNAPSHOT.json ./\\n- Verify checksum: sha256sum -c ./snapshot.manifest.sha256\\n- Postgres restore skeleton: pg_basebackup -D /var/lib/postgres/data -R -X fetch -z --verbose --label=\\\"$SNAP_ID\\\"\\n\\nNotes to self / rough TODOs:\\n- Convert this draft into a short runbook with 1-page quick start, then a detailed appendix for engineers.\\n- Pair with security on key management for archived states.\\n- Add a simple terraform module test harness for simulated state recoveries.\\n\\nEnd of draft.\\n\\n(Informal notes: lots of shorthand above, need to add specific customer examples and map to on-prem storage vendors like NetApp/CEPH, and to cloud object stores for hybrid installs. Also follow up with Marcus on the WAL retention economics spreadsheet - JIRA-PRIV-4321.)",
  "title_field_name": "title",
  "content_field_names": [
    "body"
  ],
  "dataset_doc_uuid": "dsid_67fd0fa35c704bcbac0e7aa23fcd6285"
}

    "content": "{\n  \"key\": \"SUP-19745\",\n  \"project\": \"customer-support\",\n  \"issue_type\": \"Incident\",\n  \"summary\": \"Private deployment: DNS resolution failures + TLS handshake errors after upgrade to Redwood Private 2.14.0\",\n  \"status\": \"Resolved\",\n  \"priority\": \"P1\",\n  \"severity\": \"Sev1\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2025-11-18\",\n  \"updated_at\": \"2025-11-25\",\n  \"reporter\": \"Dev Patel\",\n  \"assignee\": \"Victor Alvarez\",\n  \"customer_company\": \"Helios Bank\",\n  \"customer_tier\": \"private\",\n  \"environment\": \"prod (customer VPC, us-east)\",\n  \"affected_regions\": [\n    \"us-east (customer VPC)\"\n  ],\n  \"components\": [\n    \"private-deployments\",\n    \"networking\",\n    \"dns\",\n    \"tls\",\n    \"private-gateway\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"private\",\n    \"connectivity\",\n    \"dns\",\n    \"tls\",\n    \"upgrade\",\n    \"taxonomy-candidate\"\n  ],\n  \"first_response_due_at\": \"2025-11-18T18:00:00Z\",\n  \"sla_due_at\": \"2025-11-19T02:00:00Z\",\n  \"related_incident_id\": \"INC-2025-11-18-priv-conn-helios\",\n  \"linked_issues\": [\n    \"INT-772\",\n    \"SUP-20106\"\n  ],\n  \"related_github_prs\": [\n    \"N/A (Private release 2.14.0 bundle)\"\n  ],\n  \"related_confluence_pages\": [\n    \"confluence://eng-infra/runbooks/private-deployments/private-connectivity-dns-tls\",\n    \"confluence://eng-sre/reliability-initiatives/incident-taxonomy-v1-definitions\"\n  ],\n  \"description\": \"Issue Summary\\n- Customer reports that immediately after upgrading Redwood Private (control plane + private gateway bundle) from 2.13.2 -> 2.14.0, their application cannot reach Redwood endpoints in the private deployment.\\n- Symptoms alternate between:\\n  1) DNS resolution failures for internal Redwood hostnames (NXDOMAIN / SERVFAIL)\\n  2) TLS handshake failures when DNS does resolve (x509 / unknown authority / handshake alert)\\n\\nCustomer Impact\\n- ~65\\u201380% of requests to /v1/chat.completions and /v1/embeddings fail from the customer\\u2019s application subnets.\\n- Partial recovery observed when customer routes traffic through a different subnet / DNS forwarder.\\n- Dedicated customer-facing product endpoints impacted; customer reports degraded chatbot feature for internal employees.\\n\\nEnvironment\\n- Deployment mode: Redwood Private (customer-managed VPC, AWS us-east)\\n- Upgrade window: 2025-11-18 16:40Z\\u201317:05Z\\n- Connectivity path: app subnets -> internal DNS -> private ALB/NLB -> Redwood Private Gateway -> serving fleet\\n- Customer noted they use a split-horizon DNS setup with conditional forwarders for *.redwood.internal\\n\\nTimeline (UTC)\\n- 2025-11-18 17:12Z: Customer opens Sev1 via Support hotline; initial report: \\u201ccan\\u2019t resolve gateway hostnames; occasional TLS errors.\\u201d\\n- 2025-11-18 17:22Z: Support requests samples (dig/nslookup output, curl -v, gateway logs).\\n- 2025-11-18 17:45Z: SRE on-call pulled into #incidents (private) due to high failure rate; incident created (INC-2025-11-18-priv-conn-helios).\\n- 2025-11-18 18:15Z: Confirmed DNS failures correlate to a specific customer DNS resolver/forwarder pair.\\n- 2025-11-18 19:05Z: Confirmed TLS failures correlate to clients missing updated intermediate CA chain used by 2.14.0 gateway cert bundle.\\n- 2025-11-18 20:10Z: Workaround deployed by customer (update trust store + pin resolver); error rate drops <1%.\\n- 2025-11-19 00:30Z: Monitoring stable; incident resolved.\\n- 2025-11-25: Ticket closed after customer confirms no recurrence and completes follow-up validation.\\n\\nSteps to Reproduce (from customer)\\n1) From app host in subnet A:\\n   - dig gateway.redwood.internal A @<resolver-ip> => intermittently SERVFAIL\\n   - curl -v https://gateway.redwood.internal/healthz => sometimes: \\\"Could not resolve host\\\"; other times: \\\"SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate\\\"\\n2) From app host in subnet B:\\n   - dig consistently returns A record\\n   - curl reaches /healthz but TLS fails on older AMI hosts only\\n\\nEvidence / Logs (sanitized)\\n- DNS (intermittent):\\n  - \\\";; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: SERVFAIL\\\" (resolver <10.x.x.x>)\\n  - Occasional NXDOMAIN for gateway.redwood.internal\\n- TLS (clients on older base image):\\n  - \\\"x509: certificate signed by unknown authority\\\"\\n  - \\\"SSL routines:tls_process_server_certificate:certificate verify failed\\\"\\n- Gateway logs around upgrade window show successful cert reload and no internal errors; no elevated 5xx at gateway once requests arrive.\\n\\nInvestigation Notes\\n- We validated this is not a serving runtime regression: once traffic reaches the gateway, request success rates are normal and p95 latency is unchanged.\\n- DNS side:\\n  - Customer\\u2019s conditional forwarder for *.redwood.internal points to two internal resolvers. One resolver began returning SERVFAIL after the upgrade.\\n  - The upgrade introduced an additional internal hostname for health checks (gateway now performs an internal self-check using a new name). This increased query volume to the conditional forwarders and exposed an existing resolver capacity/config issue (SERVFAIL under modest burst).\\n  - Customer resolver logs (shared on call) show rate-limiting and a misconfigured recursion/forwarding rule for the new hostname pattern.\\n- TLS side:\\n  - Redwood Private 2.14.0 gateway cert bundle moved to a new intermediate chain (no change to leaf CN/SANs, but different intermediate). Several customer app hosts did not have the updated intermediate CA in their trust store.\\n  - Affected hosts were running an older OS image; newer image hosts validated fine.\\n\\nClassification (for Reliability Program / taxonomy validation)\\n- Proposed incident_type: Private Deployment Connectivity\\n- Proposed subtype: DNS resolution / TLS handshake\\n- Primary owner (recommended): Private Deployments\\n- Consulted: Infra/Networking (for DNS guidance), Security Ops (for cert chain/trust-store guidance)\\n- Notes: While the proximate trigger was the upgrade, the contributing factor was customer DNS forwarder config and client trust-store drift. We still track as reliability incident due to upgrade coupling + missing preflight validation.\\n\\nMitigation / Resolution\\n- Immediate mitigations applied:\\n  1) Customer pinned *.redwood.internal conditional forwarding to the healthy resolver while they adjusted the failing resolver configuration.\\n  2) Customer updated application host trust stores to include the new intermediate CA chain used by the 2.14.0 gateway cert bundle.\\n- Redwood actions:\\n  - Provided customer with the full CA chain file and verification steps.\\n  - Shared a recommended DNS preflight checklist for Private upgrades (query patterns + expected responses + suggested query rate headroom).\\n\\nCustomer Communication\\n- We confirmed no data integrity issues; this was connectivity only.\\n- We avoided asserting \\u201croot cause is customer misconfiguration\\u201d in writing; phrased as \\u201cupgrade introduced new certificate chain + additional internal DNS query pattern; existing resolver + trust-store posture was incompatible.\\u201d\\n\\nFollow-ups\\n- Support/CS:\\n  - Add this incident to the Private upgrade readiness checklist for enterprise/private customers.\\n- Engineering (requested):\\n  - Add a preflight check in Private upgrade tooling to validate:\\n    - internal DNS can resolve all required hostnames from app subnets\\n    - client trust-store compatibility (or at least detect older base images and warn)\\n  - Document cert chain changes prominently in release notes and customer upgrade guide.\\n\\nNext Update / Closure Criteria\\n- Close when customer confirms: (a) DNS stable across all resolvers, (b) TLS verification passes across all app hosts, (c) no recurrence for 5 business days.\\n\\nAttachments\\n- Customer-provided: dig/nslookup output, curl -v output (sanitized)\\n- Redwood-provided: CA chain bundle + validation steps\",\n  \"comments\": [\n    \"2025-11-18 17:18Z \\u2014 Dev Patel (Support): Opened Sev1. Customer reports post-upgrade failures: DNS SERVFAIL + TLS unknown authority. Requested dig + curl -v from two subnets and gateway endpoint details.\",\n    \"2025-11-18 17:46Z \\u2014 Rafael Mendes (SRE): Incident created (INC-2025-11-18-priv-conn-helios). Suggest classifying as Private Connectivity. Pulling in Victor for networking + Private gateway context.\",\n    \"2025-11-18 18:12Z \\u2014 Victor Alvarez (Private connectivity SME): Looking at patterns: DNS resolver intermittently SERVFAIL. Can customer share resolver IPs and conditional forwarder rules? Also confirm if gateway cert chain changed in 2.14.0 release notes.\",\n    \"2025-11-18 18:44Z \\u2014 Customer (Helios Bank): Shared outputs. Subnet A uses resolver 10.12.4.20 (SERVFAIL). Subnet B uses 10.12.4.21 (stable). TLS failures only on older AMI hosts (Amazon Linux 2 2022.03 build).\",\n    \"2025-11-18 19:07Z \\u2014 Fiona McCarthy (Security Ops): TLS error consistent with missing intermediate CA in client trust store. Recommend installing provided chain or updating ca-certificates package. Not a security incident; tracking under reliability/private connectivity is fine.\",\n    \"2025-11-18 20:15Z \\u2014 Victor Alvarez: Mitigation confirmed: customer pinned conditional forwarding to healthy resolver and updated trust store on impacted hosts. Error rate dropped to <1%. Monitoring for an hour before resolving.\",\n    \"2025-11-19 00:33Z \\u2014 Dev Patel: Marking incident resolved; keeping ticket open pending customer confirmation + follow-up checklist updates.\",\n    \"2025-11-25 16:10Z \\u2014 Dev Patel: Customer confirms stable for 5 business days, all subnets/hosts passing TLS. Closing ticket. Added note to taxonomy validation: subtype DNS/TLS under Private Deployment Connectivity; ownership primarily Private Deployments with Infra consulted.\"\n  ],\n  \"title_field_name\": \"summary\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"description\",\n    \"comments\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_cff29f8260dc414bbbbd9b00d3110e96\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Private deployment: DNS resolution failures + TLS handshake errors after upgrade to Redwood Private 2.14.0\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/jira\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/jira/customer-support/SUP-19745-private-deployment-dns-tls-errors-after-upgrade.json\nConnector: jira\nWorkspace: customer-support\nProject: customer-support\n\n##g and client trust - store drift. we still track as reliability incident due to upgrade coupling + missing preflight validation. mitigation / resolution - immediate mitigations applied : 1 ) customer pinned *. redwood. internal conditional forwarding to the healthy resolver while they adjusted the failing resolver configuration. 2 ) customer updated application host trust stores to include the new intermediate ca chain used by the 2. 14. 0 gateway cert bundle. - redwood actions : - provided customer with the full ca chain file and verification steps. - shared a recommended dns preflight checklist for private upgrades ( query patterns + expected responses + suggested query rate headroom ).",
