document.title: Private deployment: DNS resolution failures + TLS handshake errors after upgrade to Redwood Private 2.14.0
document.content:
{
  "key": "SUP-19745",
  "project": "customer-support",
  "issue_type": "Incident",
  "summary": "Private deployment: DNS resolution failures + TLS handshake errors after upgrade to Redwood Private 2.14.0",
  "status": "Resolved",
  "priority": "P1",
  "severity": "Sev1",
  "created_at": "2025-11-18",
  "updated_at": "2025-11-25",
  "reporter": "Dev Patel",
  "assignee": "Victor Alvarez",
  "customer_company": "Helios Bank",
  "customer_tier": "private",
  "environment": "prod (customer VPC, us-east)",
  "affected_regions": [
    "us-east (customer VPC)"
  ],
  "components": [
    "private-deployments",
    "networking",
    "dns",
    "tls",
    "private-gateway"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "private",
    "connectivity",
    "dns",
    "tls",
    "upgrade",
    "taxonomy-candidate"
  ],
  "first_response_due_at": "2025-11-18T18:00:00Z",
  "sla_due_at": "2025-11-19T02:00:00Z",
  "related_incident_id": "INC-2025-11-18-priv-conn-helios",
  "linked_issues": [
    "INT-772",
    "SUP-20106"
  ],
  "related_github_prs": [
    "N/A (Private release 2.14.0 bundle)"
  ],
  "related_confluence_pages": [
    "confluence://eng-infra/runbooks/private-deployments/private-connectivity-dns-tls",
    "confluence://eng-sre/reliability-initiatives/incident-taxonomy-v1-definitions"
  ],
  "description": "Issue Summary
- Customer reports that immediately after upgrading Redwood Private (control plane + private gateway bundle) from 2.13.2 -> 2.14.0, their application cannot reach Redwood endpoints in the private deployment.
- Symptoms alternate between:
  1) DNS resolution failures for internal Redwood hostnames (NXDOMAIN / SERVFAIL)
  2) TLS handshake failures when DNS does resolve (x509 / unknown authority / handshake alert)

Customer Impact
- ~65–80% of requests to /v1/chat.completions and /v1/embeddings fail from the customer’s application subnets.
- Partial recovery observed when customer routes traffic through a different subnet / DNS forwarder.
- Dedicated customer-facing product endpoints impacted; customer reports degraded chatbot feature for internal employees.

Environment
- Deployment mode: Redwood Private (customer-managed VPC, AWS us-east)
- Upgrade window: 2025-11-18 16:40Z–17:05Z
- Connectivity path: app subnets -> internal DNS -> private ALB/NLB -> Redwood Private Gateway -> serving fleet
- Customer noted they use a split-horizon DNS setup with conditional forwarders for *.redwood.internal

Timeline (UTC)
- 2025-11-18 17:12Z: Customer opens Sev1 via Support hotline; initial report: “can’t resolve gateway hostnames; occasional TLS errors.”
- 2025-11-18 17:22Z: Support requests samples (dig/nslookup output, curl -v, gateway logs).
- 2025-11-18 17:45Z: SRE on-call pulled into #incidents (private) due to high failure rate; incident created (INC-2025-11-18-priv-conn-helios).
- 2025-11-18 18:15Z: Confirmed DNS failures correlate to a specific customer DNS resolver/forwarder pair.
- 2025-11-18 19:05Z: Confirmed TLS failures correlate to clients missing updated intermediate CA chain used by 2.14.0 gateway cert bundle.
- 2025-11-18 20:10Z: Workaround deployed by customer (update trust store + pin resolver); error rate drops <1%.
- 2025-11-19 00:30Z: Monitoring stable; incident resolved.
- 2025-11-25: Ticket closed after customer confirms no recurrence and completes follow-up validation.

Steps to Reproduce (from customer)
1) From app host in subnet A:
   - dig gateway.redwood.internal A @<resolver-ip> => intermittently SERVFAIL
   - curl -v https://gateway.redwood.internal/healthz => sometimes: "Could not resolve host"; other times: "SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate"
2) From app host in subnet B:
   - dig consistently returns A record
   - curl reaches /healthz but TLS fails on older AMI hosts only

Evidence / Logs (sanitized)
- DNS (intermittent):
  - ";; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: SERVFAIL" (resolver <10.x.x.x>)
  - Occasional NXDOMAIN for gateway.redwood.internal
- TLS (clients on older base image):
  - "x509: certificate signed by unknown authority"
  - "SSL routines:tls_process_server_certificate:certificate verify failed"
- Gateway logs around upgrade window show successful cert reload and no internal errors; no elevated 5xx at gateway once requests arrive.

Investigation Notes
- We validated this is not a serving runtime regression: once traffic reaches the gateway, request success rates are normal and p95 latency is unchanged.
- DNS side:
  - Customer’s conditional forwarder for *.redwood.internal points to two internal resolvers. One resolver began returning SERVFAIL after the upgrade.
  - The upgrade introduced an additional internal hostname for health checks (gateway now performs an internal self-check using a new name). This increased query volume to the conditional forwarders and exposed an existing resolver capacity/config issue (SERVFAIL under modest burst).
  - Customer resolver logs (shared on call) show rate-limiting and a misconfigured recursion/forwarding rule for the new hostname pattern.
- TLS side:
  - Redwood Private 2.14.0 gateway cert bundle moved to a new intermediate chain (no change to leaf CN/SANs, but different intermediate). Several customer app hosts did not have the updated intermediate CA in their trust store.
  - Affected hosts were running an older OS image; newer image hosts validated fine.

Classification (for Reliability Program / taxonomy validation)
- Proposed incident_type: Private Deployment Connectivity
- Proposed subtype: DNS resolution / TLS handshake
- Primary owner (recommended): Private Deployments
- Consulted: Infra/Networking (for DNS guidance), Security Ops (for cert chain/trust-store guidance)
- Notes: While the proximate trigger was the upgrade, the contributing factor was customer DNS forwarder config and client trust-store drift. We still track as reliability incident due to upgrade coupling + missing preflight validation.

Mitigation / Resolution
- Immediate mitigations applied:
  1) Customer pinned *.redwood.internal conditional forwarding to the healthy resolver while they adjusted the failing resolver configuration.
  2) Customer updated application host trust stores to include the new intermediate CA chain used by the 2.14.0 gateway cert bundle.
- Redwood actions:
  - Provided customer with the full CA chain file and verification steps.
  - Shared a recommended DNS preflight checklist for Private upgrades (query patterns + expected responses + suggested query rate headroom).

Customer Communication
- We confirmed no data integrity issues; this was connectivity only.
- We avoided asserting “root cause is customer misconfiguration” in writing; phrased as “upgrade introduced new certificate chain + additional internal DNS query pattern; existing resolver + trust-store posture was incompatible.”

Follow-ups
- Support/CS:
  - Add this incident to the Private upgrade readiness checklist for enterprise/private customers.
- Engineering (requested):
  - Add a preflight check in Private upgrade tooling to validate:
    - internal DNS can resolve all required hostnames from app subnets
    - client trust-store compatibility (or at least detect older base images and warn)
  - Document cert chain changes prominently in release notes and customer upgrade guide.

Next Update / Closure Criteria
- Close when customer confirms: (a) DNS stable across all resolvers, (b) TLS verification passes across all app hosts, (c) no recurrence for 5 business days.

Attachments
- Customer-provided: dig/nslookup output, curl -v output (sanitized)
- Redwood-provided: CA chain bundle + validation steps",
  "comments": [
    "2025-11-18 17:18Z — Dev Patel (Support): Opened Sev1. Customer reports post-upgrade failures: DNS SERVFAIL + TLS unknown authority. Requested dig + curl -v from two subnets and gateway endpoint details.",
    "2025-11-18 17:46Z — Rafael Mendes (SRE): Incident created (INC-2025-11-18-priv-conn-helios). Suggest classifying as Private Connectivity. Pulling in Victor for networking + Private gateway context.",
    "2025-11-18 18:12Z — Victor Alvarez (Private connectivity SME): Looking at patterns: DNS resolver intermittently SERVFAIL. Can customer share resolver IPs and conditional forwarder rules? Also confirm if gateway cert chain changed in 2.14.0 release notes.",
    "2025-11-18 18:44Z — Customer (Helios Bank): Shared outputs. Subnet A uses resolver 10.12.4.20 (SERVFAIL). Subnet B uses 10.12.4.21 (stable). TLS failures only on older AMI hosts (Amazon Linux 2 2022.03 build).",
    "2025-11-18 19:07Z — Fiona McCarthy (Security Ops): TLS error consistent with missing intermediate CA in client trust store. Recommend installing provided chain or updating ca-certificates package. Not a security incident; tracking under reliability/private connectivity is fine.",
    "2025-11-18 20:15Z — Victor Alvarez: Mitigation confirmed: customer pinned conditional forwarding to healthy resolver and updated trust store on impacted hosts. Error rate dropped to <1%. Monitoring for an hour before resolving.",
    "2025-11-19 00:33Z — Dev Patel: Marking incident resolved; keeping ticket open pending customer confirmation + follow-up checklist updates.",
    "2025-11-25 16:10Z — Dev Patel: Customer confirms stable for 5 business days, all subnets/hosts passing TLS. Closing ticket. Added note to taxonomy validation: subtype DNS/TLS under Private Deployment Connectivity; ownership primarily Private Deployments with Infra consulted."
  ],
  "title_field_name": "summary",
  "content_field_names": [
    "description",
    "comments"
  ],
  "dataset_doc_uuid": "dsid_cff29f8260dc414bbbbd9b00d3110e96"
}

arguments.title: Private Deployment Rollback
arguments.content:
# Private Deployment Rollback — Fast Recovery Path

Status: candidate (not approved)
Owner: Private Deployments SRE

## Contract

Restore customer service first. The incident commander may initiate rollback as soon as a release-correlated degradation is credible; do not wait for every diagnostic artifact.

1. Open or link the incident/change ticket and name the incident commander.
2. Pause rollout widening immediately.
3. Route all traffic to the last-known-good pool and drain the candidate for 30 seconds.
4. Pin the prior signed runtime/model digest and restore the prior configuration bundle.
5. Restore state only when routing and artifact/config reversion do not recover service or when corruption is suspected. Use the newest pre-change snapshot believed clean.
6. Validate API health, 10 synthetic requests per model class, TLS/KMS checks, and latency/error recovery for 15 minutes.
7. If health remains degraded, page Private Deployments on-call and Security/Networking as indicated.
8. Record operator, timestamps, previous/new digests, snapshot ID if used, and customer communications. Complete a retrospective within 72 hours.

## Trigger

Rollback on operator-confirmed release correlation, any security regression, repeated crashes/OOM, or material customer impact. The incident commander may override metric thresholds to minimize recovery time.

## Approval

Planned rollbacks require the change owner. Emergency rollback may proceed under incident-commander authority; obtain break-glass approvals and complete evidence after service restoration.

## Network check

Before concluding the runtime is faulty, sample DNS and TLS from one affected subnet and retain the output when practical.

## Recovery objective

Prefer traffic reversion and immutable artifact pinning over state restore. Target control-plane recovery within 30 minutes.

# Private Deployment Rollback — Evidence-Gated Policy

Status: reviewed candidate
Owner: Private Deployments SRE

## Rollback contract

A rollback is a controlled production change. Protect service quickly while preserving enough evidence to choose the correct recovery layer.

### 1. Establish authority and freeze change

- Open/link the incident and change ticket; assign incident commander and rollback operator.
- Pause widening immediately. Traffic fencing is reversible and may occur while evidence is collected.
- Confirm customer rollback authority and maintenance-window contacts.
- Planned production rollback requires the recorded change approver. Emergency privileged access follows the production break-glass procedure: scoped, time-bound, fully logged, with the required two-person approval. Do not use emergency access for convenience.

### 2. Capture the minimum evidence bundle

Before artifact/config/state mutation, attach:

- candidate and last-known-good image/model digests plus config hashes;
- 15-minute pre-change baseline and current error rate, p95/p99 token latency, throughput, GPU/CPU saturation, restart/OOM, cache and quality signals;
- deployment timeline, relevant logs/traces, operator identity, and commands;
- DNS answers from every affected resolver/subnet, TLS chain verification from representative old and current client images, routes/firewall/peering exports, and gateway health;
- latest snapshot manifest, timestamp, checksum/signature result, components covered, measured restore time, and estimated data-loss window.

If evidence capture itself prolongs active harm, fence traffic to the last-known-good pool first, record why, then finish the bundle before persistent mutation.

### 3. Deterministic decision gates

Rollback when any verified release-correlated gate fires:

- p99 token latency >15% over baseline;
- 5xx above 2x baseline in canary or baseline +1 percentage point at wider ramps;
- semantic quality down >6 points on canonical prompts;
- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;
- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;
- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.

Hold the ramp for ambiguous cache misses or inconclusive network signals; isolate before mutating. A DNS/TLS failure with normal gateway/runtime health is a network/trust recovery, not evidence for runtime rollback.

### 4. Recovery sequence

1. Pause widening and route 100% away from the candidate to the last-known-good pool; drain 30 seconds.
2. Verify recovery. If successful, scale candidate to zero and preserve logs.
3. If not recovered, pin the prior signed artifact digest and restore the previous reversible config bundle.
4. Restore state only for corruption, incompatible schema/state, or failed config/artifact reversion. Use a validated clean point before the suspected corruption window.
5. For state restore: lock concurrent writers; validate manifest checksums; restore network/storage primitives, database plus WAL, control-plane metadata, model artifacts, then start in maintenance/read-only mode. Reconcile infrastructure state and require a second approver for destructive changes.
6. Re-enable writes and traffic only after API/read checks, 10 synthetic requests per model class, model checksum/quality checks, TLS and KMS verification, and 30 minutes with latency within 15% of baseline and no new OOM/restart pattern.

### 5. Closeout

Record the decision, approvals, commands, digests, snapshot IDs, evidence links, recovery/RPO impact, and customer updates. Retain rollback-window telemetry for 30 days. Produce a root-cause hypothesis within 24 hours and hold a 72-hour retrospective after threshold breach or rollback.

Private experiment: fast-recovery candidate
Assumptions/unresolved:
- Assumes incident commander can authorize emergency persistent mutation without completing the documented two-person break-glass approval.
- Uses a 15-minute validation window although published guidance commonly requires 30 minutes.
- Samples only one subnet/resolver, which can miss split-horizon DNS and trust-store drift.
- “Material impact” and operator-confirmed correlation are intentionally qualitative.
Calculations:
- Recovery target: 30m total; budget 5m fence + 10m revert + 15m validate.
- This does not reserve time for snapshot integrity verification or a full restore.
Disposition: candidate only; never index or publish this artifact.

item.text: Both branches now contain the same canonical runbook path, but with different policies, and each has a private unindexed analysis artifact. The fast path wins on immediate simplicity; the evidence-gated path better matches the documented rollback triggers, split-network failure history, snapshot integrity order, and production approval controls. I’m selecting the evidence-gated candidate without blending in the fast policy.

Protect service quickly while preserving enough evidence to choose the correct recovery layer.\n\n### 1. Establish authority and freeze change\n\n- Open/link the incident and change ticket; assign incident commander and rollback operator.\n- Pause widening immediately. Traffic fencing is reversible and may occur while evidence is collected.\n- Confirm customer rollback authority and maintenance-window contacts.\n- Planned production rollback requires the recorded change approver. Emergency privileged access follows the production break-glass procedure: scoped, time-bound, fully logged, with the required two-person approval. Do not use emergency access for convenience.\n\n### 2. Capture the minimum evidence bundle\n\nBefore artifact/config/state mutation, attach:\n\n- candidate and last-known-good image/model digests plus config hashes;\n- 15-minute pre-change baseline and current error rate, p95/p99 token latency, throughput, GPU/CPU saturation, restart/OOM, cache and quality signals;\n- deployment timeline, relevant logs/traces, operator identity, and commands;\n- DNS answers from every affected resolver/subnet, TLS chain verification from representative old and current client images, routes/firewall/peering exports, and gateway health;\n- latest snapshot manifest, timestamp, checksum/signature result, components covered, measured restore time, and estimated data-loss window.\n\nIf evidence capture itself prolongs active harm, fence traffic to the last-known-good pool first, record why, then finish the bundle before persistent mutation.\n\n### 3. Deterministic decision gates\n\nRollback when any verified release-correlated gate fires:\n\n- p99 token latency >15% over baseline;\n- 5xx above 2x baseline in canary or baseline +1 percentage point at wider ramps;\n- semantic quality down >6 points on canonical prompts;\n- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;\n- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;\n- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.",

              "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Private Deployment Rollback\nSource: Redwood Inference SRE\nPath: /knowledge/runbooks/private-deployment-rollback.md\nWorkspace: task/aisha-private-rollback-evidence\n\n6 points on canonical prompts;\n- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;\n- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;\n- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.\n\nHold the ramp for ambiguous cache misses or inconclusive network signals; isolate before mutating. # Private Deployment Rollback — Evidence-Gated Policy

Status: reviewed candidate
Owner: Private Deployments SRE

## Rollback contract

A rollback is a controlled production change. Protect service quickly while preserving enough evidence to choose the correct recovery layer.

### 1. Establish authority and freeze change

- Open/link the incident and change ticket; assign incident commander and rollback operator.
- Pause widening immediately. Traffic fencing is reversible and may occur while evidence is collected.
- Confirm customer rollback authority and maintenance-window contacts.
- Planned production rollback requires the recorded change approver. Emergency privileged access follows the production break-glass procedure: scoped, time-bound, fully logged, with the required two-person approval. Do not use emergency access for convenience.

### 2. Capture the minimum evidence bundle

Before artifact/config/state mutation, attach:

- candidate and last-known-good image/model digests plus config hashes;
- 15-minute pre-change baseline and current error rate, p95/p99 token latency, throughput, GPU/CPU saturation, restart/OOM, cache and quality signals;
- deployment timeline, relevant logs/traces, operator identity, and commands;
- DNS answers from every affected resolver/subnet, TLS chain verification from representative old and current client images, routes/firewall/peering exports, and gateway health;
- latest snapshot manifest, timestamp, checksum/signature result, components covered, measured restore time, and estimated data-loss window.

If evidence capture itself prolongs active harm, fence traffic to the last-known-good pool first, record why, then finish the bundle before persistent mutation.

### 3. Deterministic decision gates

Rollback when any verified release-correlated gate fires:

- p99 token latency >15% over baseline;
- 5xx above 2x baseline in canary or baseline +1 percentage point at wider ramps;
- semantic quality down >6 points on canonical prompts;
- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;
- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;
- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.

6 points on canonical prompts;
- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;
- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;
- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.

Hold the ramp for ambiguous cache misses or inconclusive network signals; isolate before mutating. A DNS/TLS failure with normal gateway/runtime health is a network/trust recovery, not evidence for runtime rollback.

### 4. Recovery sequence

1. Pause widening and route 100% away from the candidate to the last-known-good pool; drain 30 seconds.
2. Verify recovery. If successful, scale candidate to zero and preserve logs.
3. If not recovered, pin the prior signed artifact digest and restore the previous reversible config bundle.
4. Restore state only for corruption, incompatible schema/state, or failed config/artifact reversion. Use a validated clean point before the suspected corruption window.
5. For state restore: lock concurrent writers; validate manifest checksums; restore network/storage primitives, database plus WAL, control-plane metadata, model artifacts, then start in maintenance/read-only mode. Reconcile infrastructure state and require a second approver for destructive changes.
6. Re-enable writes and traffic only after API/read checks, 10 synthetic requests per model class, model checksum/quality checks, TLS and KMS verification, and 30 minutes with latency within 15% of baseline and no new OOM/restart pattern.

### 5. Closeout

Record the decision, approvals, commands, digests, snapshot IDs, evidence links, recovery/RPO impact, and customer updates. Retain rollback-window telemetry for 30 days. Produce a root-cause hypothesis within 24 hours and hold a 72-hour retrospective after threshold breach or rollback.

document.title: Private Deployment Rollback
document.content:
# Private Deployment Rollback — Evidence-Gated Policy

Status: reviewed candidate
Owner: Private Deployments SRE

## Rollback contract

A rollback is a controlled production change. Protect service quickly while preserving enough evidence to choose the correct recovery layer.

### 1. Establish authority and freeze change

- Open/link the incident and change ticket; assign incident commander and rollback operator.
- Pause widening immediately. Traffic fencing is reversible and may occur while evidence is collected.
- Confirm customer rollback authority and maintenance-window contacts.
- Planned production rollback requires the recorded change approver. Emergency privileged access follows the production break-glass procedure: scoped, time-bound, fully logged, with the required two-person approval. Do not use emergency access for convenience.

### 2. Capture the minimum evidence bundle

Before artifact/config/state mutation, attach:

- candidate and last-known-good image/model digests plus config hashes;
- 15-minute pre-change baseline and current error rate, p95/p99 token latency, throughput, GPU/CPU saturation, restart/OOM, cache and quality signals;
- deployment timeline, relevant logs/traces, operator identity, and commands;
- DNS answers from every affected resolver/subnet, TLS chain verification from representative old and current client images, routes/firewall/peering exports, and gateway health;
- latest snapshot manifest, timestamp, checksum/signature result, components covered, measured restore time, and estimated data-loss window.

If evidence capture itself prolongs active harm, fence traffic to the last-known-good pool first, record why, then finish the bundle before persistent mutation.

### 3. Deterministic decision gates

Rollback when any verified release-correlated gate fires:

- p99 token latency >15% over baseline;
- 5xx above 2x baseline in canary or baseline +1 percentage point at wider ramps;
- semantic quality down >6 points on canonical prompts;
- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;
- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;
- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.

Hold the ramp for ambiguous cache misses or inconclusive network signals; isolate before mutating. A DNS/TLS failure with normal gateway/runtime health is a network/trust recovery, not evidence for runtime rollback.

### 4. Recovery sequence

1. Pause widening and route 100% away from the candidate to the last-known-good pool; drain 30 seconds.
2. Verify recovery. If successful, scale candidate to zero and preserve logs.
3. If not recovered, pin the prior signed artifact digest and restore the previous reversible config bundle.
4. Restore state only for corruption, incompatible schema/state, or failed config/artifact reversion. Use a validated clean point before the suspected corruption window.
5. For state restore: lock concurrent writers; validate manifest checksums; restore network/storage primitives, database plus WAL, control-plane metadata, model artifacts, then start in maintenance/read-only mode. Reconcile infrastructure state and require a second approver for destructive changes.
6. Re-enable writes and traffic only after API/read checks, 10 synthetic requests per model class, model checksum/quality checks, TLS and KMS verification, and 30 minutes with latency within 15% of baseline and no new OOM/restart pattern.

### 5. Closeout

Record the decision, approvals, commands, digests, snapshot IDs, evidence links, recovery/RPO impact, and customer updates. Retain rollback-window telemetry for 30 days. Produce a root-cause hypothesis within 24 hours and hold a 72-hour retrospective after threshold breach or rollback.

# Private Deployment Rollback — Evidence-Gated Policy

Status: reviewed candidate
Owner: Private Deployments SRE

## Rollback contract

A rollback is a controlled production change. Protect service quickly while preserving enough evidence to choose the correct recovery layer.

### 1. Establish authority and freeze change

- Open/link the incident and change ticket; assign incident commander and rollback operator.
- Pause widening immediately. Traffic fencing is reversible and may occur while evidence is collected.
- Confirm customer rollback authority and maintenance-window contacts.
- Planned production rollback requires the recorded change approver. Emergency privileged access follows the production break-glass procedure: scoped, time-bound, fully logged, with the required two-person approval. Do not use emergency access for convenience.

### 2. Capture the minimum evidence bundle

Before artifact/config/state mutation, attach:

- candidate and last-known-good image/model digests plus config hashes;
- 15-minute pre-change baseline and current error rate, p95/p99 token latency, throughput, GPU/CPU saturation, restart/OOM, cache and quality signals;
- deployment timeline, relevant logs/traces, operator identity, and commands;
- DNS answers from every affected resolver/subnet, TLS chain verification from representative old and current client images, routes/firewall/peering exports, and gateway health;
- latest snapshot manifest, timestamp, checksum/signature result, components covered, measured restore time, and estimated data-loss window.

If evidence capture itself prolongs active harm, fence traffic to the last-known-good pool first, record why, then finish the bundle before persistent mutation.

### 3. Deterministic decision gates

Rollback when any verified release-correlated gate fires:

- p99 token latency >15% over baseline;
- 5xx above 2x baseline in canary or baseline +1 percentage point at wider ramps;
- semantic quality down >6 points on canonical prompts;
- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;
- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;
- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.",

# Private Deployment Rollback — Evidence-Gated Policy

Status: reviewed candidate
Owner: Private Deployments SRE

## Rollback contract

A rollback is a controlled production change. Protect service quickly while preserving enough evidence to choose the correct recovery layer.

### 1. Establish authority and freeze change

- Open/link the incident and change ticket; assign incident commander and rollback operator.
- Pause widening immediately. Traffic fencing is reversible and may occur while evidence is collected.
- Confirm customer rollback authority and maintenance-window contacts.
- Planned production rollback requires the recorded change approver. Emergency privileged access follows the production break-glass procedure: scoped, time-bound, fully logged, with the required two-person approval. Do not use emergency access for convenience.

### 2. Capture the minimum evidence bundle

Before artifact/config/state mutation, attach:

- candidate and last-known-good image/model digests plus config hashes;
- 15-minute pre-change baseline and current error rate, p95/p99 token latency, throughput, GPU/CPU saturation, restart/OOM, cache and quality signals;
- deployment timeline, relevant logs/traces, operator identity, and commands;
- DNS answers from every affected resolver/subnet, TLS chain verification from representative old and current client images, routes/firewall/peering exports, and gateway health;
- latest snapshot manifest, timestamp, checksum/signature result, components covered, measured restore time, and estimated data-loss window.

If evidence capture itself prolongs active harm, fence traffic to the last-known-good pool first, record why, then finish the bundle before persistent mutation.

### 3. Deterministic decision gates

Rollback when any verified release-correlated gate fires:

- p99 token latency >15% over baseline;
- 5xx above 2x baseline in canary or baseline +1 percentage point at wider ramps;
- semantic quality down >6 points on canonical prompts;
- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;
- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;
- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.

document.content:
# Private Deployment Rollback — Evidence-Gated Policy

Status: reviewed candidate
Owner: Private Deployments SRE

## Rollback contract

A rollback is a controlled production change. Protect service quickly while preserving enough evidence to choose the correct recovery layer.

### 1. Establish authority and freeze change

- Open/link the incident and change ticket; assign incident commander and rollback operator.
- Pause widening immediately. Traffic fencing is reversible and may occur while evidence is collected.
- Confirm customer rollback authority and maintenance-window contacts.
- Planned production rollback requires the recorded change approver. Emergency privileged access follows the production break-glass procedure: scoped, time-bound, fully logged, with the required two-person approval. Do not use emergency access for convenience.

### 2. Capture the minimum evidence bundle

Before artifact/config/state mutation, attach:

- candidate and last-known-good image/model digests plus config hashes;
- 15-minute pre-change baseline and current error rate, p95/p99 token latency, throughput, GPU/CPU saturation, restart/OOM, cache and quality signals;
- deployment timeline, relevant logs/traces, operator identity, and commands;
- DNS answers from every affected resolver/subnet, TLS chain verification from representative old and current client images, routes/firewall/peering exports, and gateway health;
- latest snapshot manifest, timestamp, checksum/signature result, components covered, measured restore time, and estimated data-loss window.

If evidence capture itself prolongs active harm, fence traffic to the last-known-good pool first, record why, then finish the bundle before persistent mutation.

### 3. Deterministic decision gates

Rollback when any verified release-correlated gate fires:

- p99 token latency >15% over baseline;
- 5xx above 2x baseline in canary or baseline +1 percentage point at wider ramps;
- semantic quality down >6 points on canonical prompts;
- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;
- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;
- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.

Hold the ramp for ambiguous cache misses or inconclusive network signals; isolate before mutating. A DNS/TLS failure with normal gateway/runtime health is a network/trust recovery, not evidence for runtime rollback.

### 4. Recovery sequence

1. Pause widening and route 100% away from the candidate to the last-known-good pool; drain 30 seconds.
2. Verify recovery. If successful, scale candidate to zero and preserve logs.
3. If not recovered, pin the prior signed artifact digest and restore the previous reversible config bundle.
4. Restore state only for corruption, incompatible schema/state, or failed config/artifact reversion. Use a validated clean point before the suspected corruption window.
5. For state restore: lock concurrent writers; validate manifest checksums; restore network/storage primitives, database plus WAL, control-plane metadata, model artifacts, then start in maintenance/read-only mode. Reconcile infrastructure state and require a second approver for destructive changes.
6. Re-enable writes and traffic only after API/read checks, 10 synthetic requests per model class, model checksum/quality checks, TLS and KMS verification, and 30 minutes with latency within 15% of baseline and no new OOM/restart pattern.

### 5. Closeout

Record the decision, approvals, commands, digests, snapshot IDs, evidence links, recovery/RPO impact, and customer updates. Retain rollback-window telemetry for 30 days. Produce a root-cause hypothesis within 24 hours and hold a 72-hour retrospective after threshold breach or rollback.

              "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Private Deployment Rollback\nSource: Redwood Inference SRE\nPath: /knowledge/runbooks/private-deployment-rollback.md\nWorkspace: task/aisha-private-rollback-evidence\n\n# Private Deployment Rollback — Evidence-Gated Policy\n\nStatus: reviewed candidate\nOwner: Private Deployments SRE\n\n## Rollback contract\n\nA rollback is a controlled production change.               "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Private Deployment Rollback\nSource: Redwood Inference SRE\nPath: /knowledge/runbooks/private-deployment-rollback.md\nWorkspace: task/aisha-private-rollback-evidence\n\n# Private Deployment Rollback — Evidence-Gated Policy\n\nStatus: reviewed and accepted\nOwner: Private Deployments SRE\n\n## Rollback contract\n\nA rollback is a controlled production change. Protect service quickly while preserving enough evidence to choose the correct recovery layer.\n\n### 1. Establish authority and freeze change\n\n- Open/link the incident and change ticket; assign incident commander and rollback operator.\n- Pause widening immediately. Traffic fencing is reversible and may occur while evidence is collected.\n- Confirm customer rollback authority and maintenance-window contacts.\n- Planned production rollback requires the recorded change approver. Emergency privileged access follows the production break-glass procedure: scoped, time-bound, fully logged, with the required two-person approval. Capture the minimum evidence bundle\n\nBefore artifact/config/state mutation, attach:\n\n- candidate and last-known-good image/model digests plus config hashes;\n- 15-minute pre-change baseline and current error rate, p95/p99 token latency, throughput, GPU/CPU saturation, restart/OOM, cache and quality signals;\n- deployment timeline, relevant logs/traces, operator identity, and commands;\n- DNS answers from every affected resolver/subnet, TLS chain verification from representative old and current client images, routes/firewall/peering exports, and gateway health;\n- latest snapshot manifest, timestamp, checksum/signature result, components covered, measured restore time, and estimated data-loss window.\n\nIf evidence capture itself prolongs active harm, fence traffic to the last-known-good pool first, record why, then finish the bundle before persistent mutation.\n\n### 3. Deterministic decision gates\n\nRollback when any verified release-correlated gate fires:\n\n- p99 token latency >15% over baseline;\n- 5xx above 2x baseline in canary or baseline +1 percentage point at wider ramps;\n- semantic quality down >6 points on canonical prompts;\n- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;\n- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;\n- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.",

            "content": "# Private Deployment Rollback — Evidence-Gated Policy\n\nStatus: reviewed candidate\nOwner: Private Deployments SRE\n\n## Rollback contract\n\nA rollback is a controlled production change. Protect service quickly while preserving enough evidence to choose the correct recovery layer.\n\n### 1. Establish authority and freeze change\n\n- Open/link the incident and change ticket; assign incident commander and rollback operator.\n- Pause widening immediately. Traffic fencing is reversible and may occur while evidence is collected.\n- Confirm customer rollback authority and maintenance-window contacts.\n- Planned production rollback requires the recorded change approver. Emergency privileged access follows the production break-glass procedure: scoped, time-bound, fully logged, with the required two-person approval. Do not use emergency access for convenience.\n\n### 2. Capture the minimum evidence bundle\n\nBefore artifact/config/state mutation, attach:\n\n- candidate and last-known-good image/model digests plus config hashes;\n- 15-minute pre-change baseline and current error rate, p95/p99 token latency, throughput, GPU/CPU saturation, restart/OOM, cache and quality signals;\n- deployment timeline, relevant logs/traces, operator identity, and commands;\n- DNS answers from every affected resolver/subnet, TLS chain verification from representative old and current client images, routes/firewall/peering exports, and gateway health;\n- latest snapshot manifest, timestamp, checksum/signature result, components covered, measured restore time, and estimated data-loss window.\n\nIf evidence capture itself prolongs active harm, fence traffic to the last-known-good pool first, record why, then finish the bundle before persistent mutation.\n\n### 3. Deterministic decision gates\n\nRollback when any verified release-correlated gate fires:\n\n- p99 token latency >15% over baseline;\n- 5xx above 2x baseline in canary or baseline +1 percentage point at wider ramps;\n- semantic quality down >6 points on canonical prompts;\n- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;\n- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;\n- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.\n\nHold the ramp for ambiguous cache misses or inconclusive network signals; isolate before mutating. # Private Deployment Rollback — Evidence-Gated Policy

Status: reviewed candidate
Owner: Private Deployments SRE

## Rollback contract

A rollback is a controlled production change. Protect service quickly while preserving enough evidence to choose the correct recovery layer.

### 1. Establish authority and freeze change

- Open/link the incident and change ticket; assign incident commander and rollback operator.
- Pause widening immediately. Traffic fencing is reversible and may occur while evidence is collected.
- Confirm customer rollback authority and maintenance-window contacts.
- Planned production rollback requires the recorded change approver. Emergency privileged access follows the production break-glass procedure: scoped, time-bound, fully logged, with the required two-person approval. Do not use emergency access for convenience.

### 2. Capture the minimum evidence bundle

Before artifact/config/state mutation, attach:

- candidate and last-known-good image/model digests plus config hashes;
- 15-minute pre-change baseline and current error rate, p95/p99 token latency, throughput, GPU/CPU saturation, restart/OOM, cache and quality signals;
- deployment timeline, relevant logs/traces, operator identity, and commands;
- DNS answers from every affected resolver/subnet, TLS chain verification from representative old and current client images, routes/firewall/peering exports, and gateway health;
- latest snapshot manifest, timestamp, checksum/signature result, components covered, measured restore time, and estimated data-loss window.

If evidence capture itself prolongs active harm, fence traffic to the last-known-good pool first, record why, then finish the bundle before persistent mutation.

### 3. Deterministic decision gates

Rollback when any verified release-correlated gate fires:

- p99 token latency >15% over baseline;
- 5xx above 2x baseline in canary or baseline +1 percentage point at wider ramps;
- semantic quality down >6 points on canonical prompts;
- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;
- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;
- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.

              "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Private Deployment Rollback\nSource: Redwood Inference SRE\nPath: /knowledge/runbooks/private-deployment-rollback.md\nWorkspace: task/aisha-private-rollback-evidence\n\n# Private Deployment Rollback — Evidence-Gated Policy\n\nStatus: reviewed candidate\nOwner: Private Deployments SRE\n\n## Rollback contract\n\nA rollback is a controlled production change. Protect service quickly while preserving enough evidence to choose the correct recovery layer.\n\n### 1. Establish authority and freeze change\n\n- Open/link the incident and change ticket; assign incident commander and rollback operator.\n- Pause widening immediately. Traffic fencing is reversible and may occur while evidence is collected.\n- Confirm customer rollback authority and maintenance-window contacts.\n- Planned production rollback requires the recorded change approver. Emergency privileged access follows the production break-glass procedure: scoped, time-bound, fully logged, with the required two-person approval. Do not use emergency access for convenience.\n\n### 2. Capture the minimum evidence bundle\n\nBefore artifact/config/state mutation, attach:\n\n- candidate and last-known-good image/model digests plus config hashes;\n- 15-minute pre-change baseline and current error rate, p95/p99 token latency, throughput, GPU/CPU saturation, restart/OOM, cache and quality signals;\n- deployment timeline, relevant logs/traces, operator identity, and commands;\n- DNS answers from every affected resolver/subnet, TLS chain verification from representative old and current client images, routes/firewall/peering exports, and gateway health;\n- latest snapshot manifest, timestamp, checksum/signature result, components covered, measured restore time, and estimated data-loss window.\n\nIf evidence capture itself prolongs active harm, fence traffic to the last-known-good pool first, record why, then finish the bundle before persistent mutation.\n\n### 3. Deterministic decision gates\n\nRollback when any verified release-correlated gate fires:\n\n- p99 token latency >15% over baseline;\n- 5xx above 2x baseline in canary or baseline +1 percentage point at wider ramps;\n- semantic quality down >6 points on canonical prompts;\n- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;\n- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;\n- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.",

# Private Deployment Rollback — Evidence-Gated Policy

Status: reviewed candidate
Owner: Private Deployments SRE

## Rollback contract

A rollback is a controlled production change. Protect service quickly while preserving enough evidence to choose the correct recovery layer.

### 1. Establish authority and freeze change

- Open/link the incident and change ticket; assign incident commander and rollback operator.
- Pause widening immediately. Traffic fencing is reversible and may occur while evidence is collected.
- Confirm customer rollback authority and maintenance-window contacts.
- Planned production rollback requires the recorded change approver. Emergency privileged access follows the production break-glass procedure: scoped, time-bound, fully logged, with the required two-person approval. Do not use emergency access for convenience.

### 2. Capture the minimum evidence bundle

Before artifact/config/state mutation, attach:

- candidate and last-known-good image/model digests plus config hashes;
- 15-minute pre-change baseline and current error rate, p95/p99 token latency, throughput, GPU/CPU saturation, restart/OOM, cache and quality signals;
- deployment timeline, relevant logs/traces, operator identity, and commands;
- DNS answers from every affected resolver/subnet, TLS chain verification from representative old and current client images, routes/firewall/peering exports, and gateway health;
- latest snapshot manifest, timestamp, checksum/signature result, components covered, measured restore time, and estimated data-loss window.

If evidence capture itself prolongs active harm, fence traffic to the last-known-good pool first, record why, then finish the bundle before persistent mutation.

### 3. Deterministic decision gates

Rollback when any verified release-correlated gate fires:

- p99 token latency >15% over baseline;
- 5xx above 2x baseline in canary or baseline +1 percentage point at wider ramps;
- semantic quality down >6 points on canonical prompts;
- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;
- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;
- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.

# Private Deployment Rollback — Evidence-Gated Policy

Status: reviewed candidate
Owner: Private Deployments SRE

## Rollback contract

A rollback is a controlled production change. Protect service quickly while preserving enough evidence to choose the correct recovery layer.

### 1. Establish authority and freeze change

- Open/link the incident and change ticket; assign incident commander and rollback operator.
- Pause widening immediately. Traffic fencing is reversible and may occur while evidence is collected.
- Confirm customer rollback authority and maintenance-window contacts.
- Planned production rollback requires the recorded change approver. Emergency privileged access follows the production break-glass procedure: scoped, time-bound, fully logged, with the required two-person approval. Do not use emergency access for convenience.

### 2. Capture the minimum evidence bundle

Before artifact/config/state mutation, attach:

- candidate and last-known-good image/model digests plus config hashes;
- 15-minute pre-change baseline and current error rate, p95/p99 token latency, throughput, GPU/CPU saturation, restart/OOM, cache and quality signals;
- deployment timeline, relevant logs/traces, operator identity, and commands;
- DNS answers from every affected resolver/subnet, TLS chain verification from representative old and current client images, routes/firewall/peering exports, and gateway health;
- latest snapshot manifest, timestamp, checksum/signature result, components covered, measured restore time, and estimated data-loss window.

If evidence capture itself prolongs active harm, fence traffic to the last-known-good pool first, record why, then finish the bundle before persistent mutation.

### 3. Deterministic decision gates

Rollback when any verified release-correlated gate fires:

- p99 token latency >15% over baseline;
- 5xx above 2x baseline in canary or baseline +1 percentage point at wider ramps;
- semantic quality down >6 points on canonical prompts;
- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;
- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;
- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.

Hold the ramp for ambiguous cache misses or inconclusive network signals; isolate before mutating. A DNS/TLS failure with normal gateway/runtime health is a network/trust recovery, not evidence for runtime rollback.

### 4. Recovery sequence

1. Pause widening and route 100% away from the candidate to the last-known-good pool; drain 30 seconds.
2. Verify recovery. If successful, scale candidate to zero and preserve logs.
3. If not recovered, pin the prior signed artifact digest and restore the previous reversible config bundle.
4. Restore state only for corruption, incompatible schema/state, or failed config/artifact reversion. Use a validated clean point before the suspected corruption window.
5. For state restore: lock concurrent writers; validate manifest checksums; restore network/storage primitives, database plus WAL, control-plane metadata, model artifacts, then start in maintenance/read-only mode. Reconcile infrastructure state and require a second approver for destructive changes.
6. Re-enable writes and traffic only after API/read checks, 10 synthetic requests per model class, model checksum/quality checks, TLS and KMS verification, and 30 minutes with latency within 15% of baseline and no new OOM/restart pattern.

### 5. Closeout

Record the decision, approvals, commands, digests, snapshot IDs, evidence links, recovery/RPO impact, and customer updates. Retain rollback-window telemetry for 30 days. Produce a root-cause hypothesis within 24 hours and hold a 72-hour retrospective after threshold breach or rollback.

document.content:
# Private Deployment Rollback — Evidence-Gated Policy

Status: reviewed and accepted
Owner: Private Deployments SRE

## Rollback contract

A rollback is a controlled production change. Protect service quickly while preserving enough evidence to choose the correct recovery layer.

### 1. Establish authority and freeze change

- Open/link the incident and change ticket; assign incident commander and rollback operator.
- Pause widening immediately. Traffic fencing is reversible and may occur while evidence is collected.
- Confirm customer rollback authority and maintenance-window contacts.
- Planned production rollback requires the recorded change approver. Emergency privileged access follows the production break-glass procedure: scoped, time-bound, fully logged, with the required two-person approval. Do not use emergency access for convenience.

### 2. Capture the minimum evidence bundle

Before artifact/config/state mutation, attach:

- candidate and last-known-good image/model digests plus config hashes;
- 15-minute pre-change baseline and current error rate, p95/p99 token latency, throughput, GPU/CPU saturation, restart/OOM, cache and quality signals;
- deployment timeline, relevant logs/traces, operator identity, and commands;
- DNS answers from every affected resolver/subnet, TLS chain verification from representative old and current client images, routes/firewall/peering exports, and gateway health;
- latest snapshot manifest, timestamp, checksum/signature result, components covered, measured restore time, and estimated data-loss window.

If evidence capture itself prolongs active harm, fence traffic to the last-known-good pool first, record why, then finish the bundle before persistent mutation.

### 3. Deterministic decision gates

Rollback when any verified release-correlated gate fires:

- p99 token latency >15% over baseline;
- 5xx above 2x baseline in canary or baseline +1 percentage point at wider ramps;
- semantic quality down >6 points on canonical prompts;
- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;
- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;
- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.

Hold the ramp for ambiguous cache misses or inconclusive network signals; isolate before mutating. A DNS/TLS failure with normal gateway/runtime health is a network/trust recovery, not evidence for runtime rollback.

### 4. Recovery sequence

1. Pause widening and route 100% away from the candidate to the last-known-good pool; drain 30 seconds.
2. Verify recovery. If successful, scale candidate to zero and preserve logs.
3. If not recovered, pin the prior signed artifact digest and restore the previous reversible config bundle.
4. Restore state only for corruption, incompatible schema/state, or failed config/artifact reversion. Use a validated clean point before the suspected corruption window.
5. For state restore: lock concurrent writers; validate manifest checksums; restore network/storage primitives, database plus WAL, control-plane metadata, model artifacts, then start in maintenance/read-only mode. Reconcile infrastructure state and require a second approver for destructive changes.
6. Re-enable writes and traffic only after API/read checks, 10 synthetic requests per model class, model checksum/quality checks, TLS and KMS verification, and 30 minutes with latency within 15% of baseline and no new OOM/restart pattern.

### 5. Closeout

Record the decision, approvals, commands, digests, snapshot IDs, evidence links, recovery/RPO impact, and customer updates. Retain rollback-window telemetry for 30 days. Produce a root-cause hypothesis within 24 hours and hold a 72-hour retrospective after threshold breach or rollback.

- 5xx above 2x baseline in canary or baseline +1 percentage point at wider ramps;
- semantic quality down >6 points on canonical prompts;
- GPU memory >90%, CPU steal >40%, kernel panic, GPU OOM, or >3 restarts in 5 minutes;
- throughput down >20% for 5 minutes without an external cause;
- any authentication, encryption, KMS, TLS, or integrity regression.
